prompt:
Explain the economic concept of the Equi-Marginal Principle of consumer behaviour.
(6 marks)
model_answer: The equi-marginal principle says a rational consumer with a limited income will spend it so that the marginal utility per euro (MU/P) is the same for every good bought: MU of A / Price of A = MU of B / Price of B. When the utility from the last euro spent on each good is equal, the consumer is getting the greatest total utility from their income.
marking_scheme: 6 marks (3+3). The equi-marginal principle states that consumers will spend their limited income in such a way that the ratio of marginal utility to price is the same for every good consumed, in order to maximise utility. Utility is maximised when the utility for the last euro spent on each product is equalised.

prompt:
In equilibrium, a consumer buys 6 apples at €0.90 each and 7 oranges at €0.50 each.
The marginal utility of the 6th apple is 9 utils.
Calculate the marginal utility of the 7th orange. (Show your workings.)
(10 marks)
model_answer:
In equilibrium: MU of apples / Price of apples = MU of oranges / Price of oranges.
9 / 0.90 = MU of oranges / 0.50
10 = MU of oranges / 0.50
MU of oranges = 10 x 0.50 = 5 (or 0.50 x 9 / 0.90 = 5).
Answer: the marginal utility of the 7th orange is 5 utils.
marking_scheme: 10 marks. MUA/PA = MUO/PO. 9/0.90 = MUO/0.50. MUO = 0.50(9)/0.90. MUO = 5 utils.

prompt:
Indicate whether each of the following statements is TRUE or FALSE.
1. The demand for labour is a derived demand.
2. The Live Register is the most accurate measure of Ireland's unemployment rate.
3. Cyclical unemployment is caused by a recession.
4. The backward bending labour supply curve illustrates the concept that workers substitute leisure for work as wages rise above a certain level.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
1. TRUE - labour is wanted not for its own sake but to produce goods and services people want.
2. FALSE - the Live Register counts people getting unemployment-related welfare (including some part-time workers). The Labour Force Survey is seen as more accurate.
3. TRUE - cyclical unemployment comes from the fall in demand in a downturn.
4. TRUE - above a certain wage, workers choose more leisure instead of more work.
marking_scheme: 4 @ 4 marks. 1. TRUE. 2. FALSE. 3. TRUE. 4. TRUE.

prompt:
Distinguish between the terms Economic Development and Economic Growth.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
Economic growth is an increase in income per person (e.g. GDP or GNP per capita) with no change to the structure of society. It is usually measured year on year using national income figures such as GDP, GNP or GNI.

Economic development is an increase in income per person that is accompanied by changes in the structure of society, such as better education, healthcare and infrastructure, a move from rural to urban living, or a shift from agriculture to manufacturing and services. In Ireland, free secondary education in 1967 helped development. Development takes place over many years and decades.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 8 marks, graded. Economic development refers to an increase in a country's GDP per capita / level of income / standard of living / output following a fundamental change to the structure of society, e.g. improvements in education, healthcare, infrastructure etc. Economic growth refers to an increase in a country's GDP per capita without the need for a fundamental change to the structure of society.

prompt:
Outline two main contributions to economic thought by the economist John Maynard Keynes.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
(i) Government intervention: Keynes showed that national income could settle at an equilibrium where there is not full employment. He argued that in a downturn the government should intervene using fiscal policy, raising government spending (e.g. on public works) to inject money, create jobs and boost demand. This idea shaped responses to the Great Depression.

(ii) The multiplier effect: Keynes explained that an initial injection into the circular flow of income (e.g. government spending) leads to a greater than proportionate rise in national income, because one person's spending becomes another person's income, which is then partly spent again.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 8 marks. Any two of: Favoured government intervention - national income could reach equilibrium without full employment; the best way to manage an economy efficiently was through government intervention in the form of fiscal policy. The Multiplier Effect - an initial injection into the circular flow of income leads to a greater than proportionate increase in national income. Liquidity preference theory - three motives to hold cash: transactionary, precautionary and speculative. Paradox of thrift - an increase in saving leads to a decrease in aggregate demand, which decreases national income and leads to lower total saving. Investment - could be less than savings, causing a leakage that decreases national income; investment depends more on business expectations than on the rate of interest. Rejected Say's Law (supply creates demand) - output is determined by demand, and if people do not spend enough, unemployment is caused.

topic_label: Free trade area vs customs union
prompt:
Distinguish between a Free Trade Area and a Customs Union.
(17 marks)
model_answer:
In a Free Trade Area, member countries trade freely with each other, with no tariffs or other trade barriers between them. However, each member sets its own tariffs on goods coming from non-member countries.

A Customs Union goes further. Members trade freely with each other (no tariffs between them) AND they all apply the same common external tariff to imports from countries outside the union. The EU is an example of a customs union.
marking_scheme: 11 + 6 marks. A Free Trade Area means that member countries can trade freely without tariffs / barriers being imposed on one another. A Customs Union is more advanced than a free trade area: member countries agree to trade freely and impose common tariffs on countries that are outside the union.

Tick the correct box to indicate the approximate rates which reflect the Irish Government Debt-to-GDP rate, and the Unemployment rate in the past year (this paper was set in 2019). Tick one box only in each case.
(i) Government Debt-to-GDP rate: 40% / 70% / 120%
(ii) Unemployment rate: 6% / 9% / 12%
(9 marks)
model_answer:

(ii) Unemployment rate: 6%.

prompt:
In 2019 the Irish Government Debt-to-GDP rate was approximately 70% and the Unemployment rate was approximately 6%. Explain the recent trend for each economic indicator above.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Government Debt-to-GDP rate: falling. The debt itself stayed at about €200bn, but strong economic growth made GDP bigger, so the ratio fell from a high of about 120% in 2012-2013.

Unemployment rate: falling. As the economy recovered and grew (more FDI, exports and tourism), more jobs were created and Ireland moved close to full employment.

prompt:
The Taoiseach has pledged to increase the threshold for the top rate of income tax (PAYE) to €50,000 over the next five years.
Outline two possible economic advantages and one possible economic disadvantage of this measure for the Irish economy.
(17 marks)
model_answer:
Advantages:
(i) Higher disposable income: more of a worker's income is taxed at the lower 20% rate instead of 40%, so take-home pay rises. Workers can spend more on goods and services, which improves their standard of living. This extra spending boosts demand and, through the multiplier, national income and jobs.
(ii) Incentive to work: higher take-home pay makes work more rewarding. It may encourage people to work extra hours, reduce emigration and attract skilled workers to Ireland, easing labour shortages. It may also reduce pressure for pay rises.

Disadvantage: The government will collect less income tax, so it has less revenue to spend on services such as health and education (an opportunity cost), or may have to raise other taxes.
marking_scheme: 1 @ 9 + 1 @ 4 (advantages) and 1 @ 4 (disadvantage), graded. Advantages: increased disposable income / improved standard of living; incentive to work / less emigration / increased immigration; rewards to employees are greater / more productive workforce; more equitable - the squeezed middle are better rewarded as more of their income is taxed in the lower band; greater consumer demand / multiplier effect - lower taxation reduces leakages from the circular flow; reduced pressure on wage demands - take-home pay rises without a rise in nominal wages. Disadvantages: less government revenue from taxation; opportunity cost; negative impact on the balance of payments as some extra spending goes on imports.

prompt:
In Japan 12% of the working population is aged over 65 years, whereas in the UK and Ireland the percentage is closer to 3%.
Outline two reasons why government policies might be changed to support extended working lives.
(13 marks)
model_answer:
(i) Fill labour shortages: people are living longer and are healthier because of medical advances. Keeping older people in work makes the labour force bigger, which helps fill shortages in sectors where employers cannot find enough workers.

(ii) Lower pension costs and more tax: if people work past pension age, the government delays paying them the state pension and they keep paying income tax. This improves the dependency ratio and reduces the tax burden on younger workers.
marking_scheme: 1 @ 9 + 1 @ 4 marks. Possible reasons: enlarged labour force / healthier workforce due to medical advances / helps to fill labour shortages; valuable skillset and experience; increased income tax revenue for the government; reduced government spending on pensions in the short run; recognition of a valuable part of society / retention and sharing of organisational knowledge (mentoring); improved dependency ratio, so the tax burden on those working is reduced.

prompt:
In Japan 12% of the working population is aged over 65 years, whereas in the UK and Ireland the percentage is closer to 3%.
Suggest one measure which the government or firms could take to support extended working lives.
(4 marks)
model_answer: Firms could offer flexible work arrangements to older workers, such as part-time hours, job-sharing or working from home. This lets them keep working while balancing caring roles or health needs.
marking_scheme: 4 marks. Possible measures: pension top-up schemes for those who work a minimum number of years beyond retirement age; tax breaks for individuals/firms who work/employ beyond retirement age; more flexible work arrangements (part-time, job-sharing, working from home); investment in lifelong education and training (CPD); redesigning workplaces ergonomically; promotion of an age-inclusive work culture; abolish / increase the statutory retirement age.

prompt:
Define the economic terms individual demand and market demand.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Individual demand is the quantity of a good or service that one individual consumer is willing and able to buy at different prices.

Market demand is the aggregate (total) quantity of a good or service demanded by all consumers in a market at different prices. It is found by adding up all the individual demands.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (2+3). Individual demand refers to the quantity demanded of a good or service by individual consumers at various prices. Market demand refers to the aggregate quantity demanded of a good or service by all consumers in a market at various prices.

prompt:
Outline three factors that would affect market demand for fitness watches.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
1. Tastes and preferences: as people become more health conscious and want to track their exercise, demand for fitness watches rises. Positive publicity or endorsements by influencers shift the demand curve to the right.

2. Consumer income: fitness watches are a normal good. If incomes rise, consumers can afford more of them and demand rises. If incomes fall, demand falls.

3. Price of complements and substitutes: fitness watches are used with smartphones. If phones become cheaper, demand for fitness watches rises. If a rival brand of watch cuts its price, demand for this brand falls.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible factors: change in consumer tastes / preferences (more health conscious); improved functionality / technology; successful advertising campaign; increase in consumer income / consumer confidence; change in price of the watch; change in the price of a complementary good (e.g. phones / tablets); change in the price of substitute fitness watches; expectation of future price changes; government health initiatives encouraging fitness.

prompt:
Assume the market for a brand of Irish crisps is in equilibrium. Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the effect which the following is most likely to have on the initial equilibrium position of this market:
The lack of rainfall in 2018 creates a drought which reduces potato crops.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram (described): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping demand curve D1 and an upward-sloping supply curve S1 cross at P1, Q1. A new supply curve S2 lies to the left of S1 and crosses D1 at a higher price P2 and a lower quantity Q2.

Explanation: Potatoes are the main raw material for crisps. The drought reduces the potato crop, so potatoes become scarcer and dearer. This raises the cost of making crisps, so producers supply fewer crisps at every price. The supply curve shifts to the left from S1 to S2. The equilibrium price rises from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.
marking_scheme: Diagram 5 marks: D1, S1, S2, indication of higher equilibrium price and lower quantity - 1 mark each. Explanation 5 marks: reference to reduced availability of raw materials reducing supply - 2 marks; shift of supply curve to the left, higher price, lower quantity - 1 mark each. The lack of rainfall reduces the potato crop, a raw material used in making crisps. Supply shifts left from S1 to S2. Price rises from P1 to P2. Quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.

prompt:
Assume the market for a brand of Irish crisps is in equilibrium. Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the effect which the following is most likely to have on the initial equilibrium position of this market:
Vegan consumers stage protests against animal-derived flavouring on crisps.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram (described): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. An upward-sloping supply curve S1 and a downward-sloping demand curve D1 cross at P1, Q1. A new demand curve D2 lies to the left of D1 and crosses S1 at a lower price P2 and a lower quantity Q2.

Explanation: The protests create negative publicity for the crisps, so they become less popular and consumers' tastes move away from them. Fewer crisps are demanded at every price, so the demand curve shifts to the left from D1 to D2. The equilibrium price falls from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.
marking_scheme: Diagram 5 marks: S1, D1, D2, indication of lower equilibrium price and lower quantity - 1 mark each. Explanation 5 marks: reference to negative publicity reducing demand - 2 marks; shift of demand curve to the left, lower price, lower quantity - 1 mark each. The protests create negative publicity, reducing the product's popularity. Demand shifts left from D1 to D2. Price falls from P1 to P2. Quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.

prompt:
Assume the market for a brand of Irish crisps is in equilibrium. Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the effect which the following is most likely to have on the initial equilibrium position of this market:
Crisp companies receive a subsidy from the government.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram (described): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping demand curve D1 and an upward-sloping supply curve S1 cross at P1, Q1. A new supply curve S2 lies to the right of S1 and crosses D1 at a lower price P2 and a higher quantity Q2.

Explanation: A subsidy is a payment from the government to encourage production. It lowers the crisp companies' costs of production, so they are willing to supply more crisps at every price. The supply curve shifts to the right from S1 to S2. The equilibrium price falls from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.
marking_scheme: Diagram 5 marks: D1, S1, S2, indication of lower equilibrium price and higher quantity - 1 mark each. Explanation 5 marks: reference to subsidy reducing cost of production - 2 marks; shift of supply curve to the right, lower price, higher quantity - 1 mark each. A subsidy is a payment from the government to encourage the production of a good. Supply shifts right from S1 to S2. Price falls from P1 to P2. Quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.

prompt:
The latest figures from the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) show rents continue to trend upwards, with average national rent increasing to €1,122 in Q3 2018, an increase of €78 since Q3 2017. (Source: The RTB Q3 2018 Rent Index, December 2018)
The diagram (given here in words) shows the market for rental properties. The upward-sloping supply curve and downward-sloping demand curve cross at the equilibrium rent PE, where 400,000 properties are rented. The government introduces a rent control (price ceiling), PMax, set below PE. At PMax, quantity supplied is 200,000 properties and quantity demanded is 600,000 properties.
Explain the impact of the implementation of the rent control, with reference to the diagram above.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
A rent control is a price ceiling: a maximum rent set below the equilibrium rent. Landlords cannot legally charge more than PMax.
- Before the control, the market cleared at rent PE with 400,000 properties rented.
- The rent falls from PE to PMax.
- Law of Supply: at the lower rent, renting out is less profitable, so quantity supplied falls from 400,000 to 200,000 properties.
- Law of Demand: at the lower rent, more people want to rent, so quantity demanded rises from 400,000 to 600,000.
- Result: excess demand (a shortage) of 600,000 - 200,000 = 400,000 properties.
marking_scheme: 12 marks, graded. The price has been restricted to / set at the level PMax. The price level falls from the equilibrium level PE to the new limit PMax. Quantity supplied decreased from the equilibrium quantity of 400,000 to 200,000. Quantity demanded increased from the equilibrium quantity of 400,000 to 600,000. This creates excess demand / a shortage of 400,000 (600,000 - 200,000).

prompt:
The latest figures from the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) show rents continue to trend upwards, with average national rent increasing to €1,122 in Q3 2018, an increase of €78 since Q3 2017. (Source: The RTB Q3 2018 Rent Index, December 2018)
The diagram (given here in words) shows the market for rental properties. The upward-sloping supply curve and downward-sloping demand curve cross at the equilibrium rent PE, where 400,000 properties are rented. The government introduces a rent control (price ceiling), PMax, set below PE. At PMax, quantity supplied is 200,000 properties and quantity demanded is 600,000 properties.
Outline the possible economic consequences on the Irish rental property market of this government intervention.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Fewer landlords and a shortage: with lower rental income, some landlords leave the market, so fewer properties are available. This creates excess demand and may increase homelessness, putting pressure on the government to provide housing.

2. Black market and lower quality: some landlords may charge 'cash' rents above the ceiling in the hidden economy, or add extra charges (e.g. for a parking space). With less income, landlords may also spend less on maintenance, so the quality of accommodation falls.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 4 marks (2+2). Possible consequences: improved standard of living for consumers who get a property at the lower rent; less exploitation; excess demand / shortage of properties; increased homelessness and need for government to provide accommodation; decrease in number of landlords; disimproved quality of accommodation as landlords spend less on upkeep; increase in black market activity (properties rented illegally, not declared for tax); allocation on sellers' preferences; increased utility / extra charges (e.g. for a parking space).

prompt:
Outline three characteristics of a monopoly firm.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
1. One seller: the monopolist is the only supplier in the industry, so the firm is the industry, e.g. Irish Rail.

2. Barriers to entry: new firms are kept out by barriers such as patents, very high start-up costs, economies of scale or a legal licence. This is the source of its monopoly power.

3. Downward-sloping demand curve: the monopolist can set the price or the quantity, but not both. To sell more, it must lower its price. It aims to maximise profit where MC = MR.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). 1. The firm is the sole supplier in the industry; the firm's output equals the industry output. 2. The firm seeks to maximise profits by producing where MC = MR and MC cuts MR from below. 3. The firm controls either price or quantity but cannot control both. 4. High barriers to entry prevent the entry of new firms. 5. A unique good is sold, with no close substitute (e.g. Irish Rail).

prompt:
Explain why some degree of monopoly power must exist for price discrimination to occur.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same good. To do this, a firm must be a price setter, not a price taker. If the market were competitive, rival firms selling substitutes would undercut the higher price, customers would switch, and the extra profit would be competed away. Barriers to entry stop this.
marking_scheme: 5 marks, graded. There must be some degree of monopoly / market power (price-setting power based on market share) so producers can price set rather than price take. If there were rival firms selling substitute goods, they could undercut the higher price, eliminating all demand and supernormal profits in the more expensive market.

prompt:
Explain, using a clearly labelled diagram, the long-run equilibrium position of a monopoly firm.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram (described): price/costs on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping D=AR curve; a steeper MR curve below it starting from the same point; a U-shaped AC curve; a Nike-shaped MC curve that cuts MR from below at E. From E go up to Q1 on the quantity axis; directly above, the AC curve gives cost C1 (point Y) and the D=AR curve gives price P1 (point X). The rectangle P1-X-Y-C1 is shaded as supernormal profit.

Explanation:
- Equilibrium is at E, where MC = MR and MC is rising (profit maximisation).
- The firm produces Q1 and sells it at price P1, read off the demand curve.
- The cost per unit is C1.
- Because AR (P1) is greater than AC (C1), the firm earns supernormal profits, area P1-X-Y-C1.
- Barriers to entry stop new firms entering, so these supernormal profits remain in the long run.
- The firm is not producing at the lowest point of the AC curve, so it is inefficient.
marking_scheme: Diagram 11 marks (11 @ 1): price axis, quantity axis, D=AR, MR, MC, AC, equilibrium point E, P1, Q1, C1, SNPs. Explanation 9 marks (9 @ 1): 1. Equilibrium occurs at point E where MC = MR [and MC is rising]. 2. The firm produces Q1 and sells it at P1. 3. The cost is shown at C1 (point Y). 4. The firm earns SNP (area P1, C1, Y, X) because AR > AC; it can continue to do so due to barriers to entry. 5. The firm is not producing at the lowest point on the AC curve, so it is inefficient / wasteful of resources.

prompt:
With reference to the diagram of the long-run equilibrium of a monopoly firm, explain why a firm's demand curve under monopoly differs from a firm's demand curve under perfect competition.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Monopoly: the monopolist is the only seller, so its demand curve is the market demand curve and slopes downwards. It obeys the Law of Demand: to sell more, the monopolist must lower its price. It can set the price or the quantity, but not both.

Perfect competition: each firm is one of thousands selling identical products, and each sells a tiny share of the market. The price is set by market demand and supply, and the firm must accept it (a price taker). Its demand curve is horizontal (perfectly elastic): if it raises its price even slightly, it sells nothing.
marking_scheme: 5 (2+3) + 5 (2+3) marks. Monopoly: firms face a downward-sloping demand curve; they can set the price or quantity but not both; the demand curve obeys the law of demand - to increase quantity demanded, price must fall. Perfect competition: firms face a horizontal / perfectly elastic demand curve; price is determined by market demand and supply and the firm must accept it (price-taker); firms sell homogenous goods in insignificant quantities so cannot influence the industry price.

prompt:
Big Western technology firms such as Apple, Google, Facebook and Amazon are accused of being BAADD - Big, Anti-competitive, Addictive and Destructive to Democracy. The presumption that big businesses must necessarily be wicked is plain wrong. (Source: The Economist, January 2018)
State and explain three advantages of large-scale businesses, using examples from the technology industry.
(17 marks)
model_answer:
1. Economies of scale: as large firms expand, their average cost per unit falls because of bulk buying, specialisation and automation. Lower costs can be passed on as lower prices. For example, Amazon uses huge automated warehouses and sells only online, which lowers its cost per unit.

2. Funds for research and development: large firms earn supernormal profits that can be reinvested in R&D, leading to better products over time. For example, Apple and Facebook invest heavily in improving their phones and platforms.

3. Secure employment and tax revenue: large dominant firms offer secure, well-paid jobs and pay large amounts of corporation tax, while their workers pay income tax. For example, Google employs thousands at its European headquarters in Dublin.
marking_scheme: 1 @ 9 and 2 @ 4 marks. Example required in each advantage. Possible advantages: economies of scale - lower average costs as scale increases (e.g. Amazon's large warehouses and online-only store); SNP used for R&D (dynamic efficiency) - better products at possibly lower prices (e.g. Samsung and Apple constantly updating products); less waste of scarce resources from unnecessary duplication (e.g. few companies can match Amazon); secure and attractive employment (e.g. Google's dominance means employees may not fear redundancies); guaranteed supply (e.g. Amazon and eBay dominate the online marketplace); contribution to state finances through corporation tax and employees' income tax.

prompt:
Big Western technology firms such as Apple, Google, Facebook and Amazon are accused of being BAADD - Big, Anti-competitive, Addictive and Destructive to Democracy. The presumption that big businesses must necessarily be wicked is plain wrong. (Source: The Economist, January 2018)
Outline the possible effects on a monopoly market structure of government regulation to reduce anti-competitive behaviour.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Lower prices and more output: regulators can stop the monopolist charging excessive prices, for example by approving or rejecting price increases or imposing price caps. Consumers pay less and more is produced and consumed.

2. Job losses at the old monopoly: if regulation opens the market to new firms, the former monopolist loses sales and profits and may cut staff, as can happen when an inefficient monopoly has over-hired.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 4 marks. Possible effects: reduced prices - regulators can impose price caps to stop monopolists overcharging consumers; increased quantity / choice - regulators could push firms to produce larger quantities; employment levels may be affected by the entry of new firms / restructuring of the existing firm (some job losses); poorer service - less choice, poorer service and higher 'unseen' charges.

prompt:
Explain the term Price Elasticity of Demand (PED).
(5 marks)
model_answer: Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of a good is to a change in its own price. It is the percentage change in quantity demanded resulting from a percentage change in price.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. PED refers to the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the price of the good itself / the proportionate change in the quantity demanded of a good in response to the proportionate change in the price of the good itself.

prompt:
Outline four factors that affect the PED for a good or service, providing examples to support your answer.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
1. Luxury or necessity: necessities have inelastic demand because people need them whatever the price, e.g. fuel for car owners. Luxuries are elastic because people shop around, e.g. jewellery or a new TV.

2. Close substitutes: if there are many close substitutes, demand is elastic, because a price rise makes buyers switch, e.g. one brand of cola. Few substitutes means inelastic demand, e.g. fuel.

3. Percentage of income spent: cheap items like chewing gum take a tiny share of income, so demand is inelastic. Expensive items like a car take a large share, so demand is elastic.

4. Durability: durable goods such as washing machines last for years, so buyers can postpone replacing them if the price rises. Demand is elastic.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 6 and 2 @ 4 marks. Example required in each point. Possible factors: durability (e.g. washing machines - more elastic); availability of close substitutes (e.g. butter to margarine); cheaper of two complements - inelastic (e.g. golf balls vs golf clubs); time allowed for adjustment - more elastic over time (e.g. electricity, switching to gas); luxury or necessity (e.g. doughnuts vs bread); brand loyalty - more inelastic (e.g. Apple); percentage of total income spent on the good (e.g. car vs pencil); expectation of future price changes (e.g. house prices).

prompt:
The price elasticity of demand for airline tickets from Dublin to Dubai for two different consumer categories, holiday-makers and business travellers, is given below:
PED Consumer A = -0.1
PED Consumer B = -2.4
Using your knowledge of PED, explain which figure above is more likely to correspond to holiday-makers and which to business travellers.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Consumer A (-0.1) is the business traveller. Their demand is price inelastic: they must travel for work, have few alternatives and their employer often pays. A price rise causes only a very small fall in quantity demanded.

Consumer B (-2.4) is the holiday-maker. Their demand is price elastic: a holiday is a luxury and they can choose another destination, another form of transport or not travel. A price rise causes a more than proportionate fall in quantity demanded.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (2+3). -0.1 relates to business people's demand for airline tickets as they have price inelastic demand; they have very few alternatives, so when price increases quantity demanded falls by a less than proportionate amount. -2.4 relates to holiday-makers' demand as they have price elastic demand; they view this as luxury expenditure and may look for alternative destinations, alternative modes of transport or do without, so quantity demanded falls by a more than proportionate amount.

prompt:
Explain, with the aid of diagrams, the difference between price elastic demand and price inelastic demand.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram 1 - inelastic demand (described): price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal. A steep demand curve D. A large price rise from P1 to P2 causes only a small fall in quantity from Q1 to Q2.

Diagram 2 - elastic demand (described): same axes. A flat demand curve D. A small price rise from P1 to P2 causes a large fall in quantity from Q1 to Q2.

Price inelastic demand (PED between 0 and -1): the percentage change in quantity demanded is less than the percentage change in price, e.g. necessities like fuel.
Price elastic demand (PED below -1): the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price, e.g. luxuries.
marking_scheme: Diagrams 2 @ 6 marks; explanation 2 + 2 marks. Diagram 1 shows a relatively price inelastic demand curve where PED < 1: the percentage change in quantity demanded is less than the percentage change in price. Diagram 2 shows a relatively price elastic demand curve where PED > 1: the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price.

prompt:
The price elasticity of demand for airline tickets from Dublin to Dubai for two different consumer categories, holiday-makers and business travellers, is given below:
PED Consumer A = -0.1
PED Consumer B = -2.4
Explain how knowledge of PED is useful when analysing the effect of price changes on total revenue for an airline.
(4 marks)
model_answer: Business travellers have inelastic demand, so the airline can raise their fares and total revenue will rise. Holiday-makers have elastic demand, so raising their fares would reduce total revenue; cutting fares would increase it.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 2 marks. Consumers with a price inelastic demand: if the price were increased for business passengers, the decrease in quantity demanded would be less than proportionate, so the firm would gain revenue. Consumers with a price elastic demand: if the price were increased for holiday-makers, the decrease in quantity demanded would be more than proportionate, so the firm would lose revenue.

prompt:
Assume that when the price of a tablet device was €500, consumers demanded 25,000 units of a related Good X per year. When the price of the tablet device fell to €350, the price of Good X remaining unchanged, the quantity demanded of Good X decreased to 10,000 units per year.
Calculate the cross price elasticity of demand (CED) for Good X and explain the relationship between the goods. Show your workings.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
Formula: CED = (change in Qx / change in P of tablet) x (P1 + P2) / (Qx1 + Qx2)
Change in Qx = 10,000 - 25,000 = -15,000
Change in P = 350 - 500 = -150
CED = (-15,000 / -150) x (500 + 350) / (25,000 + 10,000)
= 100 x 850 / 35,000
= 100 x 0.024286
= +2.43

The CED is positive, so the goods are substitutes. When the tablet became cheaper, consumers switched from Good X to the tablet, so demand for Good X fell. Because the figure is greater than 1, they are close substitutes.
marking_scheme: Calculation 12 marks; explanation 4 marks, graded. CED = (change in Qd of X / change in P of tablet) x (P1 + P2) / (Qx1 + Qx2) = (-15,000 / -150) x (500 + 350) / (25,000 + 10,000) = +2.42857 = +2.43. These goods are substitutes; they have a positive CED. As the price of tablet devices decreases (€500 to €350) the quantity demanded of Good X decreases (more than proportionally, 25,000 to 10,000). They are close substitutes: as the price of one falls, demand for the other falls as consumers swap from one to the other.

prompt:
Would you expect a similar cross price elasticity of demand (CED) for a tablet device and a tablet case? Explain your answer.
(4 marks)
model_answer: No. A tablet and a tablet case are complements (joint demand). If the price of tablets falls, more tablets are bought, so demand for cases rises. The CED would be negative.
marking_scheme: 4 marks, graded. No. The cross-price elasticity between these goods will give a negative sign as the goods are in joint demand (complements). If the price of one decreases, the quantity demanded of the other would increase.

prompt:
In the case of any two of the following three pairs, distinguish between the two terms:
Average Cost and Marginal Cost
Employment Rate and Participation Rate
Marginal Physical Product and Marginal Revenue Product.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Average Cost and Marginal Cost:
Average cost is the cost per unit of output: total cost divided by quantity (ATC = TC / Q).
Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one extra unit of output (MC = change in TC / change in Q).

Marginal Physical Product and Marginal Revenue Product:
Marginal physical product (MPP) is the extra output produced by employing one extra unit of a factor of production, e.g. one more worker.
Marginal revenue product (MRP) is the extra revenue a firm earns from employing one extra unit of a factor. MRP = MPP x MR.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 6 and 2 @ 4 marks. Average cost is the cost per unit of output, calculated by dividing total cost by quantity. Marginal cost is the additional cost of producing an additional unit of output. Employment rate: the proportion of the country's working-age population that is employed. Participation rate: all those in the labour force, aged 16-66, who are willing and able to work at existing wage rates, i.e. employed or seeking work. Marginal physical product: the additional output produced from the employment of an additional unit of a factor of production. Marginal revenue product: the additional revenue earned by a firm owing to the employment of an additional unit of a factor of production.

prompt:
Outline two factors which influence the Marginal Revenue Product of Labour.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
1. Skills and training of workers: skilled, well-trained and motivated workers produce more output per hour. Higher marginal physical product means a higher MRP.

2. Selling price of the output: MRP = MPP x MR. If the price the firm gets for its product rises, each worker's extra output earns more revenue, so MRP rises. If the price falls, MRP falls.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible factors: productivity / commitment of the factor (and the entrepreneur); the selling price of the output; the Law of Demand (to sell more, price must fall, reducing MRP); quality / specialised nature of the factors / unique talent; training / education provided; Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns (extra output from each additional worker eventually declines, so MRP declines).

model_answer:
A firm maximises profit where MC = MR. So we need the unit where MC = €100.

prompt:
The jobs market is currently suffering from skills shortages in the areas of accounting, engineering, pharmaceuticals, I.T. and law, amongst others. (Source: The Irish Times, November 2018)
Explain three economic effects of skills shortages for the Irish economy.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
1. Higher wages and inflation: employers compete for scarce skilled workers by offering higher pay (wage drift). This raises firms' costs of production, which may be passed on as higher prices, causing cost-push inflation.

2. Poorer services: vacancies go unfilled or are filled by less qualified recruits, so some services are delayed, not provided or of lower quality.

3. Less attractive for FDI: Ireland attracts multinationals partly because of its skilled, educated workforce. If firms cannot find the workers they need, Ireland becomes less attractive and some investment and jobs may go elsewhere.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible effects: upward pressure on wages / demand for courses in ITs and universities - higher costs for firms, cost-push inflation; reduced availability of services; deterioration in quality of services as less qualified workers are used; increased immigration (and its effects); Ireland a less attractive location for FDI, as a readily available, well-educated, English-speaking workforce is a key attraction; negative impact on productivity of Irish firms.

prompt:
The jobs market is currently suffering from skills shortages in the areas of accounting, engineering, pharmaceuticals, I.T. and law, amongst others. (Source: The Irish Times, November 2018)
Outline measures which the government and / or firms could take to address skills shortages in the Irish economy.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
1. Attract workers from abroad: the government could issue more work permits and visas for non-EU workers in shortage areas, such as the Critical Skills Employment Permit for ICT, and run schemes to encourage Irish emigrants to return home.

2. Invest in training: the government could fund free courses (e.g. Springboard), more apprenticeships and extra college places in shortage areas such as engineering and IT. More graduates would fill the gap in the labour market.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible measures: open up the Irish labour market / more efficient visa system / encourage emigrants to return / change immigration policies / encourage retired workers to return; more attractive working conditions / wages; improve access to affordable accommodation; increased student grants for education and training in areas with skill shortages; government initiatives - increased minimum wage / lower income tax rates / higher tax credits; more apprenticeship schemes to broaden the skills base.

prompt:
The Financial Times estimated that cash costs 1.5% of a country's GDP to "count it, distribute it and print it", so less cash could result in a direct improvement to the country's profitability. (Source: www.rte.ie, August 2018)
State and explain two characteristics of money.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
1. Acceptable: money must be accepted by everyone as payment for goods and services. Euro notes and coins are legal tender, so sellers must accept them.

2. Divisible: money can be broken down into smaller amounts so that small purchases can be made, e.g. a €50 note can be changed into smaller notes and coins.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (2+3). Durable - money needs to last a long time in circulation. Divisible - larger amounts can be broken down into smaller amounts for small purchases. Recognisable - genuine currency should be instantly recognisable. Acceptable - money is legal tender accepted for all goods and services. Portable - easily transported and transferred. Scarce - limited in supply so it keeps its value. Homogenous - all denominations must be identical to each other.

prompt:
The Financial Times estimated that cash costs 1.5% of a country's GDP to "count it, distribute it and print it", so less cash could result in a direct improvement to the country's profitability. (Source: www.rte.ie, August 2018)
Outline the possible advantages and disadvantages of using electronic money rather than cash for citizens and the banking industry.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Advantages:
- Citizens: convenience. Contactless payments, online banking and apps such as Revolut are quick and easy, with no need to carry cash or visit a branch. A lost card can be cancelled, but lost cash is gone.
- Banks: lower costs and higher profits. Less cash has to be counted, transported and stored, and fewer staff are needed, so banks become more efficient and profitable.

Disadvantages:
- Citizens: some people, especially older people who are not comfortable with technology, find electronic payments difficult. It is also easier to overspend or make impulse buys when you do not see cash leaving your pocket.
- Banks: security risks. Banks must spend heavily on protecting systems from hackers and on data protection, and a technology failure can stop all transactions.
marking_scheme: 4 @ 5 marks (2+3). Advantages for banks: reduced need for labour / lower staff costs; greater efficiencies and streamlined processes; more profitable. Advantages for consumers: convenience (contactless, online banking); less expensive (no travel to the bank); less crime (stolen cards can be cancelled); electronic paper trail; easier international transactions. Disadvantages for banks: security risks / hacking; data protection issues (GDPR); technological failures; human resource / IR issues as workers are replaced by technology; costs of initial set-up and maintenance. Disadvantages for consumers: difficulty for people who are not technologically proficient (especially elderly people); security risks / hacking; technological failures; possible overspending / impulse buying.

prompt:
The President of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, has outlined his intentions to increase the ECB's base interest rate from its historic low of 0%. (Source: www.ft.com, June 2018)
Given the current state of the Irish economy (2019), outline the possible arguments against an increase in the interest rate.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
1. Higher mortgage repayments: many Irish households still have large mortgages from the Celtic Tiger years. A rate rise would increase repayments on variable-rate mortgages, cut disposable income and could push some borrowers into default.

2. Less investment: higher rates raise the cost of borrowing for firms, so they invest less in capital, slowing growth.

3. Less consumer spending: higher rates reward saving, so people spend less. Lower aggregate demand means less demand for labour, and unemployment could rise again.

4. Higher cost of the national debt: Ireland's debt is over €200bn, so higher rates would raise interest payments and leave less for public services.

The current climate: inflation in Ireland is low (well below 2%), growth is uncertain because of Brexit, and debt levels are still high. There is no strong inflation to fight, so raising rates now could slow the recovery.
marking_scheme: 4 @ 4 marks (2+2) + 4 marks for linking to the current economic climate. Possible arguments: reduced investment as the cost of borrowing rises; increased cost of borrowing / mortgage interest payments; increased cost of servicing the national debt; increased incentive to save, reducing consumer spending and aggregate demand; slowing economic growth; rising unemployment as demand for goods and labour falls; risk of personal bankruptcies due to default on loans. Must link answers to the current economic climate - historic low interest rates, almost full employment, tentative economic growth, low inflation, Brexit fears, high national and individual debt, over-heating, growth of protectionism.

prompt:
Define the term government budget surplus.
(6 marks)
model_answer: A government (current) budget surplus exists when government current revenue (e.g. taxes) is greater than government current expenditure (e.g. public sector pay, social welfare). For example, Budget 2019: revenue €87.5bn minus expenditure €86.1bn = a surplus of €1.4bn.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. A government budget surplus exists when (total) government current revenue exceeds (total) government current expenditure. A budget surplus means the government has additional funds it can use.

prompt:
Outline the possible effect of a government budget surplus on a country's national debt.
(7 marks)
model_answer: The national debt is the total government borrowing still owed. With a surplus the government does not need to borrow more, and it can use the extra money to repay some of the debt. This reduces the burden on future taxpayers and lowers interest payments, freeing money for services such as health and education.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. National debt is the total (cumulative) amount of government borrowing which is outstanding. If there is a current budget surplus there are extra funds available to pay back the national debt, which reduces the debt for future generations and reduces the amount spent on servicing the debt.

prompt:
Outline how measures to reduce Ireland's national debt could conflict with any two other Irish Government objectives.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. Economic growth: to reduce debt, the government must cut spending and/or raise taxes. This takes money out of the circular flow, reduces aggregate demand and slows economic growth.

2. Improved infrastructure: projects such as hospitals, motorways and broadband need large capital spending, usually funded by borrowing. If the aim is to cut debt, these projects may be delayed or cancelled.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 6 marks (3+3). Possible conflicts: reduced national debt vs economic growth (less spending and more tax dampens growth); vs full employment (lower aggregate demand reduces demand for labour); vs improved infrastructure (capital projects are usually funded by borrowing); vs balanced regional development (less inclined to fund costly regional projects); vs redistribution of wealth (money diverted to debt reduction rather than redistribution).

prompt:
The CPI is an example of a composite price index.
Explain the steps involved in constructing a composite price index.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Choose a base year and give it an index of 100.
2. Choose a basket of goods and services that a typical household buys.
3. Collect the price of each item in the base year and the current year.
4. Work out a simple price index for each item: (current price / base year price) x 100.
5. Give each item a weight - the share of income the average consumer spends on it (from the Household Budget Survey).
6. Multiply each simple index by its weight.
7. Add the results to get the composite index.
marking_scheme: 8 marks, graded. Choose a representative base year. Decide what goods to include in the index. Gather data: find the price of each good for each time period. Construct a simple index for each commodity. Find out how much a typical consumer spends on the good as a proportion of total income, i.e. attach a weight to each good. Multiply the simple price index for each good by its weight. Add up all the results to get the overall change in prices.

prompt:
Distinguish between the terms nominal wage and real wage.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
The nominal wage is the money wage a worker is paid, before taking inflation into account.
The real wage is the money wage adjusted for inflation. It shows the purchasing power of the wage - what it can actually buy.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 4 marks. The nominal wage is the money wage (before it is adjusted for inflation). The real wage is the money wage adjusted for prices / inflation; it is the purchasing power of money.

prompt:
With reference to the table below, calculate the percentage change in real wages in each of the years 2014 - 2016. Show your workings.
Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Wage Inflation in Ireland
Year | CPI Annual % Change | Nominal Wage Rate Annual % Change | Real Wage Rate Annual % Change
2014 | 0.3 | -0.2 | ?
2015 | -0.3 | 1.2 | ?
2016 | 0.0 | 1.1 | ?
(9 marks)
model_answer:
% change in real wage = % change in nominal wage - inflation rate (CPI % change).
2014: -0.2 - 0.3 = -0.5%
2015: 1.2 - (-0.3) = 1.2 + 0.3 = +1.5%
2016: 1.1 - 0.0 = +1.1%
marking_scheme: 9 marks, graded. Real wages = nominal rate - inflation rate. 2014: -0.2 - 0.3 = -0.5. 2015: 1.2 - (-0.3) = 1.5. 2016: 1.1 - 0.0 = 1.1.

prompt:
State and explain two causes of inflation.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
1. Demand-pull inflation: when aggregate demand is greater than aggregate supply, the excess demand pulls up prices - 'too much money chasing too few goods'. This happens in boom times when incomes rise and taxes are cut.

2. Cost-push inflation: when firms' costs of production rise, such as wages, energy or raw materials, they pass these on to consumers as higher prices. Imported inflation is a form of this, where imported raw materials become dearer.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (2+3). Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand for goods and services is greater than aggregate supply; excess demand pulls up the price level. Cost-push inflation occurs when rising costs of the factors of production (without a matching rise in productivity) are passed on to consumers as higher prices; it may also take the form of imported inflation, where imported raw materials rise in price.

prompt:
Outline three possible economic effects of high inflation in an economy.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. Loss of purchasing power: each euro buys less, so living standards fall, especially for people on fixed incomes such as welfare recipients.

2. Loss of competitiveness: if Irish prices rise faster than our trading partners', Irish exports become dearer and imports cheaper, which can cost jobs in exporting firms.

3. Saving is discouraged: if inflation is higher than the interest rate, savings lose value in real terms, so people save less (while borrowing becomes more attractive).
marking_scheme: 3 @ 4 marks (2+2). Possible effects: loss of purchasing power / fall in living standards; loss of international competitiveness (harder to sell exports, more imports, damage to balance of payments); those on fixed incomes lose out (e.g. welfare recipients); saving is discouraged unless interest rates rise (and borrowing encouraged); investment skewed towards property; fiscal drag if tax bands are not indexed; demand for wage increases, raising costs for employers.

prompt:
Explain how deflation might, in the short run, lead to lower economic growth.
(8 marks)
model_answer: Deflation is a fall in the general price level. If prices are falling, consumers expect them to keep falling, so they delay purchases. Aggregate demand falls. Firms earn less, so they cut investment and output. Because labour is a derived demand, firms need fewer workers, so unemployment rises. Unemployed people spend even less, which lowers demand further and slows economic growth.
marking_scheme: 8 marks, graded. Current deflation may create the expectation that prices will keep falling, so consumers postpone consumption. As aggregate demand falls, so does the demand for labour (a derived demand). As unemployment rises, demand is dampened further, reducing economic growth (and putting further downward pressure on prices).

prompt:
National competitiveness is the ability of enterprises to compete successfully in international markets. (Source: Ireland's Competitiveness Challenge, 2018)
Outline the factors which influence Ireland's international competitiveness.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
1. Costs of production: rising energy, insurance and raw material costs are passed on as higher prices, making Irish goods and services less competitive abroad. Labour shortages push up wages too.

2. Property prices and rents: high commercial property costs make Ireland less attractive for FDI, and high rents reduce labour mobility, so firms find it harder to recruit and may need to pay more.

3. Infrastructure: poor rural broadband and traffic congestion in Dublin raise costs and cause delays, hurting efficiency.

4. Brexit and exchange rates: the UK is a key market. Uncertainty and possible tariffs, and a weaker sterling against the euro, make Irish exports dearer for UK buyers.
marking_scheme: 4 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible factors: shortage of available and affordable accommodation / rising property prices (higher costs, reduced labour mobility); infrastructure (delays to the National Broadband Plan, traffic congestion); increases in business costs - energy, utilities, insurance, inflation; Brexit uncertainty (tariff and non-tariff barriers, less investment); rising wages to attract / retain talent; under-investment in higher education; productivity gap between indigenous SMEs and foreign firms; foreign direct investment (new knowledge, skills and technology); climate action costs for firms.

prompt:
State and explain the uses of national income statistics.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. Measure economic growth and living standards: comparing national income from year to year shows whether the economy is growing and gives a general indication of whether the standard of living is rising or falling, e.g. Irish GDP fell 2008-2012 and rose from 2013.

2. Economic planning: the government uses the figures to plan policy (e.g. whether to cut taxes on labour) and then to check whether its policies worked. They are also used to work out a member state's contribution to the EU budget, which is based on GNI.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 7 marks, graded. Indication of alterations in the standard of living (also used by trade unions to justify wage demands); means of comparing the standard of living in different countries; assists the government in formulating economic policy; evaluating economic policy / benchmark to monitor progress; EU budget contributions / benefits are determined using national income statistics.

prompt:
Outline the limitations of using GDP as a measure of economic activity.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
1. Inflation: GDP can rise just because prices rise, not because more is produced. Real GDP (at constant prices) must be used to see the true change in output.

2. Activities left out: the hidden (shadow) economy, unpaid work such as stay-at-home parents and volunteering (e.g. GAA volunteers) are not counted, even though they add to welfare. GDP also ignores how income is shared - extra wealth may go to a small number of rich people - and ignores social costs such as pollution, longer commutes and stress.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 8 marks, graded. Possible limitations: population changes (national income per head); inflation / deflation; employment / unemployment; levels of taxation; exclusion of important activities (shadow / black economy, housework, voluntary work); hidden social costs (pollution, congestion) - measures flow of wealth not welfare; distribution of national income; nature of goods produced (military vs health and education); government services are valued at cost price.

Show your workings for all calculations.
Define marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
(5 marks)
model_answer: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of each extra unit of income that is spent on goods and services. MPC = change in consumption / change in income.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Marginal propensity to consume refers to the proportion of each extra unit of income which is spent on goods and services.

prompt:
Use the information in the table to answer the question below.

(5 marks)

MPS = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4
marking_scheme: 5 marks. MPS = 1 - MPC = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.

prompt:
Use the information in the table to answer the question below.
Marginal propensity to consume (MPC) | 0.6
Marginal propensity to import (MPM) | 0.2
Marginal propensity to pay tax (MPT) | 0.2
Current equilibrium level of National Income | €100 bn
Level of National Income that would give full employment | €150 bn
Show your workings for all calculations.
Calculate the value of the multiplier in this open economy and explain the economic meaning of the figure calculated.
(9 marks)
model_answer:
Multiplier = 1 / (MPS + MPM + MPT)
= 1 / (0.4 + 0.2 + 0.2)
= 1 / 0.8
= 1.25

Meaning: any injection into the circular flow of income (e.g. €1 of government spending) will increase national income by 1.25 times that amount (€1.25).
marking_scheme: Calculation 5 marks; explanation 4 marks. Multiplier = 1 / ((1 - MPC) + MPM + MPT) = 1 / (0.4 + 0.2 + 0.2) = 1.25. Any injection into the circular flow of income will have a 1.25 times larger effect on national income than the initial injection.

prompt:
Use the information in the table to answer the question below.
Marginal propensity to consume (MPC) | 0.6
Marginal propensity to import (MPM) | 0.2
Marginal propensity to pay tax (MPT) | 0.2
Current equilibrium level of National Income | €100 bn
Level of National Income that would give full employment | €150 bn
Show your workings for all calculations.
Calculate the size of the injection required to bring this economy to the full employment level.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
Rise in national income needed = €150bn - €100bn = €50bn.
Injection = rise needed / multiplier = €50bn / 1.25 = €40bn.
Answer: an injection of €40bn.

prompt:
In 2017, the Office of the Revenue Commissioners seized 125,689 litres of illicit fuel destined for sale in the shadow (black) economy. (Source: The Office of the Revenue Commissioners Annual Report, 2017)
Explain what is meant by the economic term shadow economy.
(5 marks)
model_answer: The shadow (hidden or black) economy is economic activity that is not recorded and so is not counted in national income statistics, usually to avoid tax. Examples are fuel laundering, cigarette smuggling and people working for cash without declaring it.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. The shadow economy refers to all economic activity which goes unrecorded by national income accounts.

prompt:
In 2017, the Office of the Revenue Commissioners seized 125,689 litres of illicit fuel destined for sale in the shadow (black) economy. (Source: The Office of the Revenue Commissioners Annual Report, 2017)
Outline the economic effects for Ireland of increased activity in the shadow economy.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
1. Loss of tax revenue: VAT, excise duty and income tax are not collected on shadow economy sales and earnings. The government has less money for public services, or must raise other taxes or borrow more.

2. Threat to legitimate businesses and jobs: honest firms cannot compete with illegal sellers' lower prices (e.g. a garage selling legal fuel against laundered fuel). They lose sales and may cut jobs, raising welfare costs.

3. Health and safety risks: illicit fuel and counterfeit goods follow no safety rules. Laundered fuel can damage car engines, and other goods may harm consumers. The state must also spend scarce resources on customs and Garda enforcement.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). 1. Loss of tax revenue to the government / pressure on government services - the government may have to cut spending, find other tax revenue, reduce services or borrow more. 2. Decline in legitimate business activity / threat to jobs. 3. Increased government expenditure on enforcement, putting further pressure on state finances. 4. Increased crime levels. 5. Standards of products / services - unregulated products may be unsafe / harmful to consumers.

prompt:
Budget 2019 failed to increase carbon taxes. Environmentalists viewed this as a missed opportunity for the government to underline its commitment to environmental protection.
Explain the terms progressive tax and regressive tax providing an example in each case.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
A progressive tax takes account of ability to pay: it takes a higher percentage of income from high earners than from low earners. Example: PAYE income tax, with a 20% standard rate and a 40% higher rate.

A regressive tax takes a higher percentage of income from low earners than from high earners, because everyone pays the same amount regardless of income. Example: VAT - €100 of VAT is a third of a €300 weekly income but only a sixth of a €600 weekly income.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 5 marks (4 + 1: explanation 4, example 1). A progressive tax takes a higher proportion from high income earners than from low-income earners; the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises, e.g. income tax (PAYE). A regressive tax takes a higher proportion from low income earners than high-income earners; the proportion paid falls as income increases, e.g. VAT, as rich and poor pay the same amount of tax on the goods they buy.

prompt:
Budget 2019 failed to increase carbon taxes. Environmentalists viewed this as a missed opportunity for the government to underline its commitment to environmental protection.
In your opinion, did the government make the correct decision in failing to increase carbon taxes in Budget 2019? Support your answer with relevant economic information.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
No, I think the government made the wrong decision.

1. Polluter pays: fossil fuels create negative externalities (carbon emissions and climate change) that fall on society. A higher carbon tax makes the users of these fuels pay for the damage and reduces demand for them.

2. EU targets: Ireland is falling short of its EU emission reduction targets. Raising the carbon tax would bring Ireland closer to them and help avoid penalty payments.

3. Encourages a green switch and raises revenue: higher fuel prices make public transport, electric vehicles and home insulation relatively more attractive. The extra revenue could fund grants for EVs or insulation, or be used to protect low-income and rural households, who are hit hardest because the tax is regressive.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). Yes: not needed for revenue as the government is already running a surplus; it is regressive and hits low-income earners harder (they spend a higher share of income on heating and transport fuel); adds to business costs, conflicting with job creation, reducing inequality and attracting investment; harms export competitiveness; firms, individuals and state authorities need time to adjust; anti-rural due to lack of public transport. No: the fuels are demerit goods that harm the environment; polluter pays principle; government is failing to meet EU environmental targets and could avoid penalty payments; it would raise additional revenue for state services; it would encourage a switch to sustainable energy and preserve non-renewable resources.

prompt:
The key message from the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC) on Budget 2019 was that there were repeated failures by the government to prevent unbudgeted government spending. (Source: IFAC Fiscal Assessment Report, November 2018)
Outline the possible negative economic effects of the government's repeated overspending.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
1. Budget deficits and more debt: repeated overspending can turn a surplus into a deficit, so the government must borrow. This adds to the national debt, which future taxpayers must repay with interest.

2. Higher future taxes: to pay for the overspending and the extra interest, taxes may have to rise in future, reducing disposable income and demand.

3. Loss of credibility: if the government cannot control its own budgets, its plans lose credibility at home and abroad. This could damage Ireland's international reputation and credit rating, raising the interest rate it pays when borrowing.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible effects: risk of future budget deficits (departments expect extra funding, leading to inaccurate planning); risk of accumulating additional debt, creating opportunity costs for future spending; need for higher future taxation; uncertainty and lack of credibility in government planning; deterioration in quality of service provision in other departments; damage to Ireland's international reputation and credit rating.

prompt:
Ireland's corporation tax rate of 12.5% is one of the lowest in the EU.
Outline three possible economic effects on the Irish economy of increasing the corporation tax rate.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
1. Less FDI: the 12.5% rate is a key reason over 1,500 multinationals locate here. A higher rate could make other countries more attractive, so some firms might leave and fewer new ones would come.

2. Job losses: if multinationals leave or do not expand, direct and indirect jobs would be lost, raising unemployment and the social welfare bill.

3. Uncertain effect on tax revenue: firms that stay would pay more corporation tax, so revenue may rise at first. But if firms leave, the government loses corporation tax, income tax and VAT. On the positive side, it could improve Ireland's reputation, as some claim Ireland is a tax haven.
marking_scheme: 3 @ 5 marks (2+3). Possible effects: loss of FDI / difficulty attracting new FDI as MNCs consider cheaper locations or relocate to the US; loss of employment and a higher social welfare bill; effects on government revenue - less corporation tax, income tax and VAT if firms leave, though firms that stay pay more, possibly a temporary rise in tax collected; extra spending needed to promote Ireland for FDI; a more equitable taxation system - possible lower personal taxation and an improved international reputation.

prompt:
Calculate the balance of trade for the period 2015 - 2019.
Identify whether it is a surplus or a deficit.

Ireland's Exports and Imports 2015-2019 (Adapted from the CSO)
Period | Exports (€'s millions) | Imports (€'s millions)
2015 | 112 | 70
2016 | 119 | 74
2017 | 123 | 83
2018 | 141 | 92
2019 | 152 | 91
(7 marks)
model_answer:
Step 1: Add the exports: 112 + 119 + 123 + 141 + 152 = €647 million.
Step 2: Add the imports: 70 + 74 + 83 + 92 + 91 = €410 million.
Step 3: Balance of trade = exports - imports = €647m - €410m = €237 million.
Answer: €237 million. Exports are greater than imports, so it is a trade SURPLUS.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. Total exports: 112 + 119 + 123 + 141 + 152 = 647. Total imports: 70 + 74 + 83 + 92 + 91 = 410. €647m - €410m = €237m. Trade surplus.

prompt:
Outline two reasons why achieving a trade surplus is an objective of the Irish government.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Increased employment: when demand for Irish exports rises abroad, Irish firms need more workers to produce these goods, so employment in exporting firms rises.
2. Economic growth: exports are an injection into the circular flow of income. Through the multiplier effect, this money is re-spent, giving a more than proportional rise in national income and a better standard of living. Imports, by contrast, are a leakage, so a surplus means more money flows in than out.
marking_scheme: 8 marks: 2 points @ 4 marks (descriptor marking). Points include: Increased employment - more demand for Irish exports abroad means more demand for Irish labour to produce the goods, increasing Irish employment. Injection into the circular flow / economic growth - exports are an injection into the circular flow of income and may create a multiplier effect, a more than proportional increase in national income, more employment and a better standard of living. Imports are a leakage from the circular flow - they may create a negative multiplier effect, reducing national income and creating foreign jobs in place of Irish jobs.

prompt:

The table below shows the subscription price for a basic Netflix account in different countries. (The prices have been converted into US dollars $ for comparison purposes)
Country | Netflix Subscription per month (US $)
Switzerland | 12.3
Ireland | 8.7
Australia | 5.9
Denmark | 11.6
Rwanda | 8.0
(Adapted from Statista)

(a) Outline one reason why consumers are willing to pay different prices for a Netflix subscription in different countries.
(b) Other than your answer given in part (a) explain two other conditions necessary for price discrimination to occur in this scenario.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
(a) Consumer indifference: Netflix customers in Switzerland may know that people in Australia pay less, but they do not mind. They feel the service is worth $12.30 a month to them rather than go without it.
(b) 1. Monopoly power: Netflix must have some monopoly power. If customers saw Disney+ or Amazon Prime as perfect substitutes, rivals would undercut the high prices and the price discrimination would end.
2. Separate markets with different price elasticities: Netflix must be able to keep the markets apart so that a customer cannot buy in a cheap country (Australia) and resell in a dear one (Switzerland). Each country must also have a different price elasticity of demand, so Netflix charges more where demand is inelastic (Switzerland) and less where it is elastic (Australia).
marking_scheme: 15 marks for the whole question (the published scheme does not show the split between (a) and (b)). (a) Consumers accept price discrimination for 3 possible reasons: 1. Consumer ignorance - the consumer is unaware the price discrimination is taking place. 2. Consumer indifference - consumers are aware but don't care. 3. Consumer attitudes - consumers feel it is worth paying more rather than go without. (b) Monopoly power - the firm must have some monopoly power, otherwise rivals would undercut prices; consumers must see rivals such as Disney+ and Amazon Prime as imperfect substitutes for Netflix. Different price elasticities of demand - the firm must recognise that customers in different countries are more/less responsive to price changes and price accordingly, e.g. Switzerland most inelastic, Australia most elastic. Market separation (no arbitrage) - it must be impossible for customers to buy in the cheaper market and resell in the dearer market, undercutting Netflix.
source: 2021 State Exam - Section A, Q3 (a) and (b)

prompt:
In budget 2021, the price of a 20 pack of cigarettes rose from €13.50 to €14.00. Cigarettes are classed as 'Demerit Goods' and as such their purchase constitutes a market failure.

(a) Explain your understanding of the economic term Demerit Goods.
(7 marks)
model_answer: A demerit good is a good that can harm the person who consumes it. Consumers overestimate the benefit and underestimate (or do not know) the harm. If it is over-consumed it also creates negative externalities: costs that fall on third parties who did not consume it, e.g. a non-smoker who becomes ill from passive smoking, or the cost to the health system of treating smokers.
marking_scheme: 7 marks (4 + 3). Demerit goods are goods whose positive effect is overestimated by consumers and which have negative effects which consumers possibly underestimate or are unaware of. Demerit goods usually also have negative externalities, i.e. negative effects on third parties not involved in the consumption of the good.

prompt:
In budget 2021, the price of a 20 pack of cigarettes rose from €13.50 to €14.00. Cigarettes are classed as 'Demerit Goods' and as such their purchase constitutes a market failure.

Answer (b) or (c)
(b) Explain why the purchase of demerit goods, such as cigarettes, is seen as a market failure.
(8 marks)
model_answer: Market failure is when a free market allocates goods inefficiently. Left to the free market, cigarettes could cost about €3 a packet. This price does not include the full cost to society: treating smokers' illnesses, treating non-smokers made ill by passive smoking, and cleaning up cigarette litter. Because the price is too low to reflect the true private and social cost, people over-consume a harmful product.
marking_scheme: 8 marks (4 + 4). The free market will lead to the production and overconsumption of a harmful good, because the market price fails to reflect the true private or social cost of the product. If the free market took full account of the private and social costs, the price would be much higher.

prompt:
In budget 2021, the price of a 20 pack of cigarettes rose from €13.50 to €14.00. Cigarettes are classed as 'Demerit Goods' and as such their purchase constitutes a market failure.

Answer (b) or (c)
(c) Explain why the Irish Government intervenes by imposing higher taxes on cigarettes in budgets.
(8 marks)
model_answer: The government taxes cigarettes to raise their price. By the Law of Demand, a higher price reduces consumption of a product that harms smokers and creates negative externalities for others, such as passive smoking. About €11 of the €14 price is tax. The tax revenue can also pay for the costs smoking causes, e.g. treating smoking-related illness in hospitals and funding the HSE Quitline. The revenue earned can help fund the cost of dealing with the negative externalities, e.g. over-crowding of healthcare services. Left to the free market, the price would be too low to reflect the true private and social cost, leading to overconsumption of a harmful product.

prompt:

(7 marks)
model_answer: GDP only measures the total value of output in a country, so it shows the level of economic activity, not how well people live. The HDI is a composite index that combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita). Because it includes health and education as well as income, it gives a fuller picture of human welfare.

It considers more variables that affect human welfare. GDP only reflects the level of economic activity within the country.

prompt:
John always spends his income in the following ratio of price to marginal utility:
MUx/Px = 2500/200 = MUy/Py = 1250/100 = MUz/Pz = 75/?

(a) Calculate the price John would be willing to pay for one unit of good Z.
(b) Explain why John would pay this price.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
(a) Step 1: MUx/Px = 2500 / 200 = 12.5.
Step 2: MUy/Py = 1250 / 100 = 12.5.
Step 3: MUz/Pz must also equal 12.5, so 75 / Pz = 12.5.
Step 4: Pz = 75 / 12.5 = 6.
Answer: John would pay €6 for one unit of good Z.
(b) John is a rational consumer who wants to maximise his total utility from his limited income. Under the equi-marginal principle, he gets the most utility when the marginal utility per euro spent (MU/P) is equal for every good. At €6, good Z gives 12.5 utils per euro, the same as goods X and Y, so paying €6 keeps his utility at its maximum.
marking_scheme: 15 marks for the whole question (the published scheme does not show the split between (a) and (b)). (a) 2500/200 = 12.5; 1250/100 = 12.5; 75 / 12.5 = 6. Price of Z = €6 (written as 75/6). (b) He would pay this price in order to maximise his utility, as he spends his income in line with the equi-marginal principle of consumer behaviour, i.e. the ratio of marginal utility to price is the same for every unit of every good consumed.
source: 2021 State Exam - Section A, Q8 (a) and (b)

marking_scheme: 8 marks (3 + 5). Highly concentrated because: the HHI is greater than 2,500; 92% of the market share is shared between two firms; the industry is dominated by two firms.

prompt:
A firm is in long-run equilibrium in Oligopoly at point E, producing at Q1 and selling at P1 (kinked demand curve).

(b)(ii) Would you advise the above firm to engage in price competition? Give two reasons for your answer.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
No, I would not advise price competition.
1. Price war: oligopoly firms are interdependent. If this firm cuts its price, rivals will match the cut, starting a price war that lowers profits for everyone.
2. No gain in revenue: below the kink, demand is relatively inelastic because rivals match price cuts. A price cut brings a less than proportionate rise in sales, so total revenue falls. The firm is already earning supernormal profits, so it should use non-price competition such as advertising instead.
marking_scheme: 8 marks: 2 @ 4 marks. Answer: No. Reasons: Fear of a price war - if a firm decreases price, rivals will also decrease theirs. No increase in total revenue - cutting price on an inelastic demand curve gives a less than proportionate rise in quantity demanded, so revenue falls. Firms currently earning supernormal profits - changing price will not increase revenue and may raise costs, reducing profits. Menu costs - constant price changes bring extra costs, e.g. reprinting menus.

(b)(iii) Outline two reasons why small firms such as Embraer and Bombardier may survive in this market.
