prompt:
Boeing and Embraer entered potential merger talks in 2019. If a merger were to occur between Boeing and Embraer it is likely they would benefit from Internal Economies of Scale.

(c)(i) Define Internal Economies of Scale.
(c)(ii) Outline possible Internal Economies of Scale which could arise for Boeing and Embraer if this merger were to occur.
(26 marks)
model_answer:
(i) Internal economies of scale are the cost savings within a firm that cause its cost per unit (average total cost) to fall as the firm increases its scale of production.
(ii) 1. Purchasing economies: the merged firm would buy steel, engines and components in much larger quantities and could negotiate bulk-buying discounts, lowering the cost per unit.
2. Specialisation of labour: with a bigger workforce, each worker can focus on one task and become very efficient, raising productivity and cutting costs.
3. Financial economies: a larger firm is a more important and safer customer for banks, so it can borrow more easily and at lower interest rates.
4. Technical economies: by pooling resources, the merged firm can afford the most advanced machinery and assembly lines, reducing the cost of producing each aircraft.
5. Managerial and marketing economies: only the best managers from both firms are kept, and one specialist marketing team can promote a wider range of aircraft, spreading these costs over more output.
marking_scheme: 26 marks for part (c) in total (the published scheme does not show the split between (i) and (ii)). (i) Internal economies of scale refer to the decreases in average total cost accruing to a firm as it increases its scale of production. (ii) Labour economies - more specialisation of workers, higher productivity, lower costs. Managerial economies - only the best managers kept, cutting administrative costs. Purchasing economies - bulk buying of raw materials lowers per unit costs. Technical economies - pooling resources to afford the most advanced technology. Economies in use of raw materials - the same basic components on all aircraft, less waste. Economies in distribution - more locations, reduced transport costs. Marketing economies - marketing cost spread over a wider output; one specialist team. Financial economies - access to more finance and lower interest rates.
source: 2021 State Exam - Section B, Q11 (c)(i) and (ii)

prompt:
(a)(i) Explain the term globalisation.
(4 marks)
model_answer: Globalisation is the process by which the world's economies are becoming more interconnected and interdependent, through the flow of goods, services, people, culture and knowledge across borders.
marking_scheme: 4 marks. Globalisation is the process by which the world is becoming increasingly interconnected as a result of massively increased trade and cultural exchange; an increasing internationalisation of markets for goods and services, the means of production, financial systems, competition, corporations, technology and industries. The ability to produce any good or service anywhere in the world, using inputs from anywhere, sell anywhere and place the profits anywhere.

prompt:
(a)(ii) Outline two positive impacts and two negative impacts of globalisation.
(26 marks)
model_answer:
Positive 1 - Economies of scale and lower prices: access to bigger world markets lets firms grow and gain economies of scale. Lower costs can be passed on as lower prices, making goods such as mobile phones affordable to people on low incomes.
Positive 2 - Jobs and economic growth: global firms create jobs directly and indirectly. For example, Intel is investing €3.63 billion in Leixlip, which raises national income and tax revenue.
Negative 1 - Economic shocks spread: because economies are interdependent, a crisis in one country spreads. The collapse of Lehman Brothers in the US in 2008 helped cause a deep recession in Ireland.
Negative 2 - Damage to the environment: flying and shipping goods around the world greatly increases carbon emissions, and some governments allow pollution to keep multinationals happy.
marking_scheme: 26 marks: four impacts, two marked @ 8 (5 + 3) and two marked @ 5 (2 + 3). Positive: trade enhances division of labour (specialisation in areas of comparative advantage raises productivity); improvements in economic growth and higher per capita incomes; reduction in numbers living in extreme poverty; innovation is encouraged and greater variety of goods; benefits of economies of scale and more competitive prices. Negative: inequality (rising Gini coefficient, rural-urban divide); re-location of jobs / exploitation of workers and structural unemployment; increases in world food prices; dominant global brands / small firms may disappear; threat to the environment; trade imbalances and pressure for protectionism; macroeconomic instability (e.g. 2008 credit crunch contagion); standardisation of commodities / loss of individual cultures.

prompt:
In Budget 2020, the Minister for Finance reaffirmed Ireland's commitment to the 12.5% corporation tax rate.

(b)(i) Evaluate two reasons why the Minister for Finance made this decision.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. To attract and keep FDI: the 12.5% rate is much lower than in France (28-31%) or Germany (30%) and has helped attract over 1,500 foreign firms to Ireland. If the rate rose, multinationals might move some or all of their operations elsewhere, and future investment could be cancelled. Keeping the rate is therefore very important.
2. To protect jobs and tax revenue: IDA-supported firms employ over 245,000 people directly, and for every 10 FDI jobs about 8 more indirect jobs are created. Corporation tax raised €10.9 billion in 2019. A higher rate could reduce both jobs and revenue, although relying so heavily on a few large firms is also a risk.
marking_scheme: 14 marks: 2 @ 7 marks (3 + 4). Points: Incentivise FDI / discourage any exodus of MNCs - the low rate has historically attracted foreign firms; a higher rate might make them leave. Maintain employment levels. Government revenue - corporation tax is a large part of tax receipts and finances state services. Maintain economic growth - FDI and employment are essential for stable growth. Loss of fiscal sovereignty - Ireland has already ceded monetary policy to the EU and does not want to cede its other main macroeconomic tool.

prompt:
In Budget 2020, the Minister for Finance reaffirmed Ireland's commitment to the 12.5% corporation tax rate. The Irish government has repeatedly rejected calls from the European Commission to remove Ireland's ability to set its own corporation tax rate.

(b)(ii) Outline one reason why the European Commission want to remove this power from the Irish government.
(7 marks)
model_answer: The European Commission sees Ireland's low rate as an unfair, anti-competitive advantage. Other EU countries miss out on FDI because multinationals put their European headquarters in Ireland to pay 12.5% instead of much higher rates elsewhere. The Commission wants more consistent tax policies across the EU.
marking_scheme: 7 marks (3 + 4). One of: Streamlining of all European policies (social, environmental, economic) - Ireland's corporation tax policy is seen as out of line with the rest of Europe. Greater transparency across the EU - e.g. the €13bn in unclaimed taxes from Apple. Seen as anti-competitive - Ireland's rate is an outlier; some members view it as an unfair advantage.

prompt:
The United Kingdom exited the European Union on January 31, 2020.

(c)(i) Discuss two implications of this exit for the Irish economy.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. Exports and trade costs: the UK is one of Ireland's most important trading partners, especially for agri-food. Even with the December 2020 trade deal, extra paperwork and checks mean extra costs and possible delays at ports. Many exporters also use the UK as a land bridge to Europe, so Irish exports become dearer and less competitive.
2. Relocation of firms: UK firms that sell into the EU have an incentive to move to Ireland, now the only English-speaking EU country. For example, Barclays moved operations from London. This brings new jobs and investment to Ireland.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 2 @ 6 marks (3 + 3). Points: Possible negative effect on Irish exports - about 15% of goods and services exports go to the UK, around 40% of agri-food exports; two-thirds of exporters use the UK land bridge. Effects on agriculture / agri-food - reduced preferential access to the UK market; tariffs, customs costs and regulatory divergence; fishing may fare badly. Labour market effects - some export sectors may lose jobs, but foreign firms relocating from the UK could create jobs. Imports from the UK - dearer due to tariffs and customs costs; dearer raw materials; supply chain disruption; consumers may switch online shopping to EU sites.

prompt:
The United Kingdom exited the European Union on January 31, 2020.

(c)(ii) Outline two possible advantages to Ireland of remaining a member of the EU.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. Access to a large free market: Irish firms can sell goods and services to around 448 million people in the EU with no tariffs or quotas. This lets them expand, gain economies of scale and employ more people.
2. Attracting FDI: foreign firms, especially from the US, locate in Ireland to get free access to the EU market. This creates jobs and raises tax revenue. Since Brexit, Ireland is the only English-speaking EU country, which makes it even more attractive.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 2 @ 6 marks (3 + 3). Points: Free trade area / larger market - access to over 500 million people tariff free; collective EU trade agreements. Access to capital / research funding - infrastructure, retraining grants, Erasmus. Freedom of movement of capital / labour - live and work anywhere in the EU; qualifications recognised. Foreign Direct Investment / job creation - Ireland as an export hub for American firms. EU legislation and policies - CAP, Fisheries Policy, European Health Insurance Card. Supports the Peace Process - PEACE Programmes, about €2.26 billion since 1995.

prompt:
Shortages of the PlayStation 5 Gaming Consoles (PS5) was a nightmare for many consumers in the lead up to Christmas 2020. (Adapted from Forbes)
The retail price for a PlayStation 5 Gaming Console was €500. In part (a)(i) a demand and supply diagram was completed showing excess demand in this market at the €500 price.

(a)(ii) From your diagram above, explain how excess demand occurs.
(12 marks)
model_answer: Excess demand happens when the price is set below the equilibrium price. At €500, the quantity demanded (QX) is greater than the quantity supplied (QE), and supply of PS5s was fixed in the short run. The gap between QX and QE is the excess demand: unsatisfied customers who cannot get a console. The €500 price is too low. The shortage signals that the price should rise. As price rises towards the equilibrium price P1, quantity demanded falls and the shortage disappears, because the higher price rations the scarce consoles.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 3 @ 4 marks. At the price of €500 there is more demand (QX) than the available (fixed) supply of the product (QE). This indicates the price charged is too low; the excess demand puts upward pressure on price, driving it to the equilibrium price P1. By undercharging for the PS5 it created additional demand which would be rationed if the price were increased.

prompt:
Technology retailers mislead shoppers with Black Friday 'deals'. A survey of 'before and after' pricing shows that many products are not discounted as claimed. (Adapted from the Irish Independent)

(b)(i) Explain why misinformation to consumers by technology retailers represents a market failure in this industry.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Market failure is an inefficient allocation of resources in a free market. Imperfect information is one cause. Here there is asymmetric information: the retailer knows the real 'before' price but the shopper does not. Shoppers are misled into thinking they are getting a bargain, so they buy products at exploitative prices and misallocate their limited income.
marking_scheme: 6 marks (3 + 3). Information failure is a form of market failure because the consumer does not have access to information the retailer is aware of. This asymmetric information puts the consumer at a disadvantage and makes them more likely to be exploited. Retailers knowingly giving pricing misinformation means consumers are purposely misled, more likely to buy at exploitative prices and misallocate their resources. Note: market failure occurs when the price mechanism leads to an inefficient or inequitable allocation of resources.

prompt:
Technology retailers mislead shoppers with Black Friday 'deals'. A survey of 'before and after' pricing shows that many products are not discounted as claimed. (Adapted from the Irish Independent)

(b)(ii) Evaluate how Government intervention in this market could address this market failure.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
1. Regulation and stronger penalties: the government can pass laws requiring honest advertising, as with the Sale of Goods and Supply of Services Act, and give the regulator (the CCPC) power to investigate and fine retailers who mislead shoppers. If penalties are large and enforcement strong, retailers will be deterred, although this costs the taxpayer money to run.
2. Better information for consumers: the government can fund awareness campaigns and websites such as citizensinformation.ie, and require retailers to publish price histories. Informed shoppers are harder to mislead, which tackles the root cause, asymmetric information.
marking_scheme: 10 marks: 2 @ 5 marks (2 + 3). Points: Increased public awareness - more resources for sites such as citizensinformation.ie so consumers are less likely to be exploited. Government legislation/regulation and enforcement - e.g. amend the Consumer Protection Act 2007. Increased penalties for offenders - higher chance of being caught and bigger penalties deter offenders. Increased accuracy of information - require firms to publish annual product price lists so consumers can track prices.

prompt:
(b)(iii) Explain, giving an example, one advantage of a government regulation.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Regulation prevents anti-competitive behaviour and so protects consumers from being exploited. For example, the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) investigates price fixing and can block mergers. Ryanair was prevented from taking over Aer Lingus, which kept competition and lower fares for consumers.
marking_scheme: 6 marks: 2 @ 3 marks (explanation and example). Points: Health and safety regulations - consumers protected from substandard and unsafe products. Protects consumers from exploitation by large firms earning supernormal profits. Prevents anti-competitive behaviour / growth of monopolies - ends cartels; assesses mergers. Increases competition in the industry. Environmental protection - less resource use and pollution. Employment laws - safe working environments and proper pay.

prompt:
Apple AirPods (earphones) price fell from €160 to €125 online. The quantity demanded increased from 10,000 units to 15,000 units.

(c)(i) Calculate the Price Elasticity of Demand of Apple AirPods.
(15 marks)

Apple AirPods (earphones) price fell from €160 to €125 online. The quantity demanded increased from 10,000 units to 15,000 units. The Price Elasticity of Demand is -1.63.

(c)(ii) Based on the figure you have calculated in (i) above, state whether the demand for Apple AirPods is elastic or inelastic. Give a reason for your answer.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Answer: Elastic (relatively elastic).
Reason: the PED of -1.63 is greater than 1 when we ignore the minus sign. This means the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price.
marking_scheme: 8 marks (4 + 4). Elastic. Reason: the number is greater than 1 (in absolute terms); the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price.

prompt:
Apple AirPods (earphones) price fell from €160 to €125 online. The quantity demanded increased from 10,000 units to 15,000 units. The Price Elasticity of Demand is -1.63 (elastic).

(c)(iii) If a firm selling the above product intends to maximise revenue from the sale of this product should it, increase, decrease or maintain the same price? Explain your answer.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Answer: Decrease the price.
Explanation: demand is elastic, so a price cut leads to a more than proportionate rise in quantity demanded. For example, the fall from €160 to €125 raised revenue from €1.6 million (160 x 10,000) to €1.875 million (125 x 15,000). So cutting price increases total revenue.
marking_scheme: 10 marks. As demand is elastic the firm should decrease price to increase total revenue. A decrease in price leads to a more than proportionate increase in quantity demanded, thereby increasing total revenue.

2. Ireland's rate fell from 0.4% in 2014 to -0.3% in 2016 (deflation), while the UK's rate began rising after 2015.

prompt:
The graph below shows the Harmonised Indices of Consumer Prices (HICP) average inflation rate - Ireland, UK and Euro Area 2014-2019. (Adapted from Eurostat - Irish Competitiveness Council Scorecard)
Year | UK (%) | Ireland (%) | Euro Area (%)
2014 | 1.5 | 0.4 | 0.45
2015 | 0.0 | 0.2 | 0.4
2016 | 0.8 | -0.3 | 0.4
2017 | 2.7 | 0.4 | 1.6
2018 | 2.5 | 0.6 | 1.7
2019 | 1.9 | 0.7 | 0.9

(a)(ii) Outline the potential advantages to Ireland as a country of maintaining the lowest price inflation rate relative to these other areas over this period.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. More competitive exports: when Irish prices rise more slowly than prices in the UK and the Euro Area, Irish goods and services become relatively cheaper abroad. Demand for Irish exports rises, creating more jobs in exporting firms, and more tourists may choose to holiday in Ireland.
2. Lower costs and wage restraint: low inflation keeps firms' costs down and reduces pressure from workers for pay rises, because their purchasing power is not being eroded. Lower costs make Ireland more attractive for FDI and protect the value of people's savings.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 2 @ 6 marks (3 + 3). Points: More competitive exports - Irish prices lower than Euro area and UK, so more exports and employment; more tourists. Competitive costs - lower costs for Irish firms help them expand/innovate; incentive for foreign firms to locate here. Domestic spending / savings / wage restraint / reduced demand for imports - encourages spending at home; maintains value of savings; Irish people holiday at home. Government finances - more spending, exports and employment improve government finances.

prompt:
(b)(i) Outline two possible disadvantages to Irish citizens of a low inflation rate in Ireland.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. Consumers postpone spending: if prices are rising very slowly or falling, people delay purchases while waiting for lower prices. Demand falls, some firms may close or cut staff, and consumers may lose services.
2. Heavier burden of debt: with low inflation, the money borrowers repay keeps its value, so the real burden of mortgages and other loans does not shrink. Households with large mortgages are worse off than they would be with higher inflation. Employers may also offer little or no pay rise.
marking_scheme: 14 marks: 2 @ 7 marks (3 + 4). Points: Consumers may postpone spending, expecting prices to fall further; some firms may close. No / low wage increases - employers offer low or no pay rises. Debt burden effect - the real cost of repaying loans (mortgage and state debt) rises. Asset appreciation rate may fall - homes and investments do not rise in value as quickly.

prompt:
(b)(ii) Explain one method the government could use to address rising inflation.
(7 marks)
model_answer: The government could use contractionary fiscal policy by increasing direct taxes on labour, such as PAYE or USC. This reduces people's disposable income, so consumer spending and aggregate demand fall. With less money 'chasing too few goods', demand-pull inflation is reduced.
marking_scheme: 7 marks (3 + 4). One of: Increase direct taxation - less income, so consumers spend less, reducing demand-pull inflation. Decrease government current expenditure - government spending is an injection; cutting it reduces aggregate demand and demand-pull inflation. Reduce the cost of government-provided utilities - lowers firms' production costs and so cost-push inflation.

prompt:
(c)(i) Define the principle of comparative advantage.
(6 marks)
model_answer: The principle of comparative advantage states that a country should specialise in the goods and services it can produce relatively most efficiently, that is, at the lowest opportunity cost compared with other countries, and trade for the rest.
marking_scheme: 6 marks (3 + 3). Comparative advantage is the ability of a country to produce a particular product at a lower opportunity cost than another country. It reflects the relative opportunity cost. It drives countries to specialise in goods for which they have the lowest opportunity cost, which leads to increased productivity.

prompt:
Continued capital investment in the National Broadband Plan in Ireland is one of the National Competitiveness Council recommendations for 2020. (Adapted from Ireland's Competitiveness Scorecard 2020)

(c)(ii) Discuss the importance of this recommendation for Ireland's international competitiveness.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. Attracting FDI: multinationals need high-speed broadband to connect with world markets. Good infrastructure, including broadband, is one reason Ireland attracts over 1,500 foreign firms. Poor rural broadband would make Ireland less attractive than competing countries.
2. Lower business costs and flexible working: fast broadband lets firms trade online, order supplies more cheaply and take payments electronically, cutting costs. During Covid-19 it allowed people to work from home so business continued. Firms in rural areas can sell online and expand, making Irish exports more competitive.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 2 @ 6 marks (3 + 3). Points: Ability to attract FDI - companies need high-speed broadband to connect with world markets. More flexible working arrangements - working from home during Covid-19 needs high-quality broadband nationwide. Allows the state to provide services more efficiently online, lowering costs. Reduces costs of running a business - manage activities online, source cheaper supplies, meet orders quickly, electronic payment; rural firms can trade online and expand.

prompt:
(c)(iii) Choose two other areas the Irish Government should focus on to increase its international competitiveness. Justify your choice in each case.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. Education and training: a skilled workforce lowers recruitment and training costs for firms and makes workers more productive. Funding courses in shortage areas such as IT (e.g. Springboard) helps fill vacancies without pushing up wages.
2. Tackling the housing shortage: high rents and house prices make it hard for firms to recruit, reduce labour mobility and push workers to demand higher wages. Building more homes would lower housing costs, ease wage pressure and make Ireland more attractive for FDI.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 2 @ 6 marks (3 + 3). Points: Fund skills, education and training programmes; improve infrastructure for business (transport, ports, airports, water); manage the housing shortage (reduce housing costs and pressure for wage increases); support enterprise/entrepreneurship (finance, less red tape); reduce utility charges and insurance costs; encourage competition / deregulation; reduce taxation / maintain the 12.5% CPT rate; address climate action in a competitiveness context.

prompt:
(a) Which measure is a more accurate indicator of Ireland's economic welfare: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) or Gross National Income (GNI)? Justify your answer.
(21 marks)
model_answer:
Answer: GNI.
Justification: GDP measures the value of all output produced in Ireland, by both Irish-owned and foreign-owned factors of production. Ireland has over 1,500 foreign multinationals, and much of their profit is repatriated to their home countries. This income is in Irish GDP but is not shared among Irish residents, so GDP overstates Irish living standards. Moving intellectual property to Ireland and inversion deals made GDP jump by 26% in 2015, which clearly did not reflect real living standards.
GNI measures the income earned by Irish residents and businesses wherever it is earned. It subtracts the profits, wages and interest sent abroad by foreign factors (net factor income is negative), and adds EU subsidies less EU taxes. In 2019 GDP was €356bn but GNI was only €275bn, about one-fifth lower. GNI therefore gives a much more accurate picture of Irish economic welfare.
marking_scheme: 21 marks (7 + 7 + 7). GNI is a more accurate measure of the economic welfare of Irish citizens as it is income received by permanent domestic residents. It excludes incomes generated by the owners of a large part of the capital stock who are non-residents. The level of GNI is over one-fifth lower than GDP. GDP measures total incomes arising from production in Ireland; a significant part accrues to foreign owners of capital, so GDP overstates the living standards of Irish residents. Key: GNI = income to permanent domestic residents / excludes incomes to foreign owners of capital.

prompt:
(b)(i) Define the term recession.
(8 marks)
model_answer: A recession is a fall in a country's GDP (negative economic growth) for at least two successive quarters, that is, two three-month periods in a row.
marking_scheme: 8 marks (4 + 4). A recession refers to a period of negative economic growth lasting at least two quarters.

model_answer:
Years: 2007 to 2009.
Explanation: in both countries GNI per capita fell during this period. Ireland fell from $52,000 in 2007 to $44,000 in 2009, and the US fell from $56,500 to $54,000. Falling national income shows both economies were shrinking, which means they were in recession.
marking_scheme: 8 marks (4 + 4). The period from 2007 to 2009 sees both countries experience an economic recession. During this period the GNI of both countries is downward sloping, indicating the size of their economies was shrinking, i.e. experiencing a recession.

prompt:
(b)(iii) With reference to GNI, why is it important to use per capita measures for comparisons between countries?
(8 marks)
model_answer: Total GNI does not take account of population size. Two countries with the same GNI could have very different living standards if one has many more people. GNI per capita (GNI divided by population) shows the average income per person, so it is a fairer comparison. For example, if GNI doubles but the population also doubles, income per person has not changed at all.
marking_scheme: 8 marks. GNI per capita takes account of the populations of the countries being compared; two countries with similar GNI may have very different standards of living because of different population sizes. Comparing nominal GNI only may over-estimate the standard of living/economic growth; if population rose, income per person may actually have fallen. Worked example: Country A GNI $400m to $500m with population 4m to 5m - income per person unchanged at $100; Country B GNI $100m to $150m with 1,000 people - income per person rises from $100,000 to $150,000.

prompt:
(c)(i) Explain the term multiplier.
(8 marks)
model_answer: The multiplier means that an injection into the circular flow of income (e.g. government spending) causes a more than proportionate rise in national income, because one person's spending becomes another person's income, which is spent again. For example, with a multiplier of 2, a €100m injection raises national income by €200m.
marking_scheme: 8 marks. The multiplier effect means that any injection into the circular flow of income leads to a more than proportionate increase in national income, e.g. an initial injection of €100m will lead to a €200m increase in national income if the multiplier is 2.

prompt:
(c)(ii) Assume that MPM is 0.25 and MPC is 0.65 and MPT is 0.10. Calculate the multiplier. Show all your workings.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Step 1: MPS = 1 - MPC = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35.
Step 2: Formula for an open economy with a government sector: Multiplier = 1 / (MPS + MPM + MPT).
Step 3: 1 / (0.35 + 0.25 + 0.10) = 1 / 0.70.
Step 4: 1 / 0.70 = 1.43.
Answer: Multiplier = 1.43.

prompt:
(c)(iii) Discuss two possible negative multiplier effects of large corporations such as Google withdrawing from their rental property contracts in Dublin city during 2020.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. Lost rents: the owners of the office buildings no longer receive rent from Google. Their income falls, so they spend less. This lost spending is someone else's lost income, and the fall in national income is multiplied through the economy.
2. Less spending in local businesses: Google's employees no longer buy lunches, coffees and services near the offices. Cafes, shops and transport firms lose revenue, may cut staff, and those workers then spend less too. Lower activity also means less VAT and income tax for the government, deepening the negative multiplier effect.
marking_scheme: 14 marks: 2 @ 7 marks (3 + 4). Points: Lost rents - property owners lose rental income and spending power, a negative multiplier effect. Reduced demand for goods and services - local businesses lose the custom of Google's employees, so less revenue and spending; employment falls. Reduced demand for public transport - transport companies lose income, possible job losses. prompt:
Using an appropriate formula, calculate the price elasticity of demand depicted in the graph below where the original price of the packet of face masks is €4 and then increases to €5. Show all calculations.
DEMAND FOR FACE MASKS
Quantity demanded | Price in euro €
2 | 6
4 | 5
8 | 4
20 | 1
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Formula: PED = (change in Q / change in P) x (P1 + P2) / (Q1 + Q2).
At €4, quantity demanded = 8. At €5, quantity demanded = 4.
Change in Q = 4 - 8 = -4. Change in P = 5 - 4 = +1.
PED = (-4 / 1) x (4 + 5) / (8 + 4)
= -4 x 9/12
= -4 x 0.75
= -3.
Answer: PED = -3. Demand is relatively elastic.

prompt:
Firms can survive in the short run even if they are making a loss. Explain this statement.
(7 marks)
model_answer: In the short run a firm still has to pay its fixed costs (e.g. rent, insurance) even if it closes. If its price (AR) covers its average variable cost (AVC), the extra revenue pays all variable costs and part of the fixed costs. Shutting down would mean losing all of the fixed costs, which is a bigger loss. So the firm keeps producing in the short run.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. In the short run, if AR is greater than AVC the firm is making a loss, but once it covers its average variable costs it will contribute towards its fixed costs. The loss from shutting down would then be greater than the loss from continuing to operate. (The published scheme does not show the mark split for this part clearly; the marks given here are an estimate.)

prompt:
In the long run only the most efficient firms will survive. Explain this statement.
(7 marks)
model_answer: In the long run new firms enter until price falls to the lowest point of the average cost curve, where AR = AC and firms earn only normal profit. A firm must earn at least normal profit to stay in business. A firm whose costs are above the lowest point of AC makes a loss at this price and must leave. So only efficient firms survive.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. A firm is most efficient when it is producing at the minimum point of AC. If it is not producing at the minimum point of the average total cost curve in the long run it is not being efficient. It will not be earning normal profit and so will be forced, due to inefficiency, to leave the industry. (10 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram: Price on the vertical axis and Quantity of land on the horizontal axis. Draw a vertical supply curve S at quantity QE, because land is fixed in supply (perfectly inelastic). Draw a downward-sloping demand curve D. They cross at E, giving price PE.
Explanation: supply of land cannot change, so price is decided by demand. PE is where demand equals the fixed supply. If demand rises, the price of land rises but quantity stays at QE.
marking_scheme: Diagram: Price (vertical axis), Quantity (horizontal axis), vertical supply curve S, downward-sloping demand curve D, equilibrium E, price PE, quantity QE. Explanation: the supply of land is fixed in quantity at S. The demand for land is downward sloping from left to right (D). The equilibrium price PE is established where D is equal to S. prompt:
Explain, with the use of a fully labelled diagram, the long-run equilibrium position of a monopoly firm.
(19 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram: Price on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal. A downward-sloping D/AR curve with a steeper MR curve below it. A U-shaped AC curve and a Nike-shaped MC curve. MC cuts MR from below at E. From E go up to Q1. Go up from Q1 to the D/AR curve to find P1, and to the AC curve to find C1. The rectangle between P1 and C1 is supernormal profit (SNP).
Explanation:
1. Output: the firm maximises profit where MR = MC, at Q1.
2. Price: P1, read off the demand curve.
3. Efficiency: cost C1 is not at the lowest point of AC, so the firm is inefficient.
4. Profit: AR is greater than AC, so it earns supernormal profit. Barriers to entry stop new firms entering, so it keeps this profit in the long run.
marking_scheme: 19 marks: diagram 11 marks (1 mark per label: Price, Quantity, P1, Q1, C1, E, D/AR, MR, MC, AC, SNP) + explanation 8 marks. Explanation points: the firm produces where MR = MC (and MC cuts MR from below) at Q1; they sell the output at price P1; inefficiency occurs as costs are not at the minimum point of the AC curve; AR > AC so supernormal profits are earned in the long run because barriers to entry prevent new firms entering. (The published scheme does not show the mark split for this part clearly; the marks given here are an estimate.)

Product differentiation exists in oligopoly - firms spend heavily to convince consumers their product is superior and avoid price wars; in monopoly none of this is necessary.

The Irish government uses both direct and indirect tax to raise government revenue. Distinguish between these two types of taxes. Use examples of each to support your answer.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
Direct taxes are taxes on income and wealth. They are paid directly to the government by the person who earns the income. Many are progressive, taking a higher percentage from high earners.

Indirect taxes are taxes on spending on goods and services. The consumer pays them as part of the price and the seller passes them to the government. They are regressive.

marking_scheme: 16 marks: (6 + 2) + (6 + 2). Direct taxes are taxes placed upon income and wealth, e.g. PAYE and capital gains tax. Indirect taxes are taxes placed on spending on goods and services, e.g. VAT and excise duties.

(6 marks)

When MC is below AC, AC is falling.
When MC is above AC, AC is rising.
When MC equals AC, AC is at its minimum. So the rising MC curve cuts the U-shaped AC curve at its lowest point.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. When marginal cost is greater than average cost, average cost is rising. When marginal cost is less than average cost, average cost is falling. When marginal cost equals average cost, average cost is at a minimum.

Explain, with the use of a fully labelled diagram (including the axes), the long run equilibrium of a firm in perfect competition.
(17 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram: Price on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal axis. A horizontal line D = AR = MR at price P. A U-shaped AC curve whose lowest point just touches the D = AR = MR line. A Nike-shaped MC curve cutting MR from below at that same point, E. A dotted line drops from E to quantity Q. Price P and cost C are at the same level.
Explanation: the firm produces where MR = MC, at point E, giving output Q. It sells at the market price P, as it is a price taker. Cost per unit is C, which equals P, so AR = AC and the firm earns normal profit only. Any supernormal profit has been competed away by new firms entering. The firm produces at the lowest point of the AC curve, so it is efficient.
marking_scheme: Diagram 9 marks (1 mark per label: Price, Quantity, P, C, Q, MC, AC, D/AR/MR, E). Explanation 8 marks: equilibrium is at point E (where MC = MR); firms produce quantity Q; they sell at price P; costs occur at level C; the firm earns normal profit as AR = AC; the firm is efficient as costs are at the minimum point of the AC curve.

prompt:
Explain the terms injections and leakages and refer to two examples of each from your diagram of the Circular Flow of Income for an open economy.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
Injections: money that enters the circular flow from outside household spending. They increase aggregate demand and national income, by the injection times the multiplier.
Examples: government spending; exports.
Leakages: income that is not spent on the output of domestic firms. They take money out of the circular flow and reduce national income.

Mar-21 7.6; Apr-21 7.1; May-21 7.0; Jun-21 6.5; Jul-21 5.9; Aug-21 5.6; Sep-21 5.3; Oct-21 5.1; Nov-21 5.2; Dec-21 5.0; Jan-22 4.8; Feb-22 4.9; Mar-22 4.9; Apr-22 4.6; May-22 4.2; Jun-22 4.1; Jul-22 4.2; Aug-22 4.3; Sep-22 4.4.
From the graph above analyse one trend in Ireland's monthly unemployment rate from March 2021 to September 2022, using figures from the above graph.
(8 marks)
model_answer: Overall the unemployment rate fell. It dropped from 7.6% in March 2021 to 4.4% in September 2022, a fall of 3.2 percentage points. The lowest point was 4.1% in June 2022. After that it rose slightly to 4.4%. The fall reflects the economy reopening after Covid-19 restrictions.
marking_scheme: Part (a) carries 26 marks; this part inferred at 8. Trend with figures, e.g. between March 2021 and September 2022 the rate fell from 7.6% to about 4.4%, a decrease of 3.2%; or between March 2021 and May/June 2022 it fell from 7.6% to about 4.2%; or between mid-2022 and September 2022 it rose slightly, e.g. from 4.2% to 4.4%.

prompt:
Another method of measuring unemployment is the Quarterly National Household Survey (now the Labour Force Survey). Give two reasons why this measure is considered more accurate than data collected from the Live Register.
(4 marks)
model_answer:
1. The Live Register counts some part-time workers who get a partial payment, so they appear fully unemployed.
2. The survey uses a large sample of households and asks if people are actually available for and seeking work.
marking_scheme: 4 marks (awarded to all candidates who attempted this question, as the question should have referred to the Labour Force Survey). The Live Register includes those receiving a partial social welfare payment (part-time workers counted as fully unemployed); some on the Live Register work full time in the hidden economy and illegally claim welfare; some are voluntarily unemployed and not actively seeking work; the Labour Force Survey uses a large sample size - the larger the sample, the more accurate the results.

prompt:
Describe two types of unemployment giving examples to support your answer.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. Structural unemployment: a mismatch between the skills of the unemployed and the jobs available. It happens when an industry declines or technology replaces jobs. Example: a supermarket checkout operator replaced by self-service checkouts, or peat workers after Bord na Mona stopped harvesting peat.
2. Cyclical unemployment: caused by a fall in demand for goods and services during a downturn in the business cycle. Firms need fewer workers. Example: unemployment rose sharply in 2008 after the financial crisis and in 2020 during Covid-19.
marking_scheme: 14 marks: 2 @ 7. Structural - mismatch between skills of the unemployed and jobs available, e.g. jobs made obsolete by technology; frictional - time taken moving between jobs, e.g. a person between jobs; seasonal - at certain times of the year, e.g. tourism workers in winter; cyclical - downturn reduces demand, e.g. Covid-19 job losses; institutional - caused by institutional arrangements, e.g. a high minimum wage.

prompt:
Explain the economic term full employment.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Full employment is when everyone in the labour force who is willing and able to work can find a job at existing wage rates. An unemployment rate of about 4% is seen as full employment.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Full employment refers to a situation in which all those members of the labour force who are willing and able to work are employed (4) at existing wage rates (2).

prompt:
Maintaining full employment is an objective of the government. Outline two other current economic objectives of the government in 2023, and justify your answers.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Control the price level: inflation was high in 2022 and 2023, cutting real incomes. Keeping prices stable protects living standards.
2. Build more houses: there is a housing shortage and high rents, so more supply is needed to reduce homelessness and help workers move for jobs.
marking_scheme: 8 marks: 2 @ 4. Build more houses / reduce homelessness; control the price level; achieve sustainable economic growth; achieve social sustainability / reduce inequality; achieve environmental sustainability; balanced regional development; increase international trade/competitiveness; maintain state services e.g. health; improve national infrastructure; maintain fiscal stability; maintain stability in the financial sector; intervention/regulation to alleviate market failures / during national emergencies.

prompt:
The Irish government spent €8.8bn on the Pandemic Unemployment Payment (PUP) in 2021. (Adapted from gov.ie)
Use a cost-benefit approach to assess who enjoyed the private benefit, the external benefit and who bore the costs of this scheme.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
Private benefit: workers who lost their jobs due to Covid-19 got an income (initially €350 a week) to pay for food, rent and bills.
External benefit: recipients kept spending, so shops and other businesses could stay open and keep staff. The government also got back some VAT on that spending.
Who bore the costs: the government borrowed to fund it, adding to the national debt. Current and future taxpayers must repay this with interest.
marking_scheme:
12 marks: 3 @ 4.
Private benefit: people left unemployed received a basic income to survive / money to spend on goods and services.
External benefit: the government received tax revenue from citizens' spending; continued spending allowed some businesses to remain open.
Who bore the cost: the government had to borrow to fund the scheme, some from European institutions; Irish taxpayers must fund this into the future.

prompt:
In the 1950s and 1960s, Ireland had a very high rate of unemployment. During this period policy makers favoured trade protection.
Explain the economic term trade protection.
(7 marks)
model_answer: Trade protection is when a government uses barriers such as tariffs, quotas and embargos to restrict imports. The aim is to protect domestic firms and jobs from foreign competition.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. Trade protection refers to government policies involving the imposition of trade barriers such as tariffs which deliberately reduce/restrict international trade in the hope of protecting domestic production and employment.

prompt:
Some countries are now favouring a return to trade protection measures. Discuss two economic reasons why countries are favouring a return to trade protection.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Protect domestic jobs: tariffs make imports dearer, so consumers buy more home-produced goods and jobs are kept at home.
2. Less reliance on other countries: Covid-19 showed the danger of depending on imports for essential goods like PPE from China, so countries want more self-sufficiency.
marking_scheme: 8 marks: 2 @ 4. Reduce leakages from the circular flow (imports); protect domestic employment; reduce pollution from transport of imports; less reliance on foreign markets; political/strategic reasons, e.g. Brexit, sanctions over the war in Ukraine.

prompt:
Outline two possible disadvantages of trade protection.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Higher prices: consumers pay the tariff through dearer imports, and domestic firms face less competition so they can charge more.
2. Retaliation: other countries may put tariffs on our exports, as China did against the US in 2018, which harms exporters and jobs.
marking_scheme: 8 marks: 2 @ 4. Stagnation of technological advances - no incentive to innovate or invest in R&D, no economies of scale; reduced choice for consumers; increase in prices due to lack of competition; reduction in economic growth / damage to employment if many countries protect; economic isolation and retaliation / trade wars.

prompt:
The diagram shows the average electricity price charged to Irish households (2020-2022), in € cent per kWh (S = Semester; adapted from SEAI):
2020 S1 23.1; 2020 S2 25.0; 2021 S1 24.0; 2021 S2 28.2; 2022 S1 26.5.
Outline one key trend in electricity prices, using figures from the graph above and explain how this will have impacted on Irish consumer behaviour.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
Trend: prices rose overall, from 23.1c per kWh in 2020 S1 to 26.5c in 2022 S1, a rise of 3.4c. The peak was 28.2c in 2021 S2.
Effect on consumers: higher electricity bills reduce the purchasing power of household income. Real incomes fall, so consumers have less to spend on other goods. Those on fixed incomes, such as social welfare, are hit hardest. Many households try to cut their electricity use.
marking_scheme: Part (a) total 32 marks; this part inferred at 12 (trend with figures + effect). Trend: overall upward trend from S1 2020 to S1 2022, or an individual trend with figures (e.g. 2021 S2 to 2022 S1). Impact on consumers: purchasing power reduced - standard of living falls as real wages fall; those on fixed incomes (e.g. social welfare) suffer; purchasing power of savings reduced if inflation exceeds the interest rate, reducing the incentive to save; burden of debt reduced - borrowing encouraged.

prompt:
Distinguish between demand-pull inflation and cost-push inflation.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Demand-pull inflation: aggregate demand is greater than aggregate supply. Too much money chases too few goods, pulling prices up.
Cost-push inflation: costs of production such as wages, energy and raw materials rise, and firms pass these on as higher prices.
marking_scheme: 8 marks (2 + 2 each). Cost-push inflation occurs when increases in costs of production (2) are passed on to the consumer in the form of higher prices (2). Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand is greater than aggregate supply (2) leading to upward pressure on prices (2).

prompt:
The table below shows a country's composite price index for the following categories of expenditure: food; transport; and other items. Use the information in the table below to calculate the price index for the current year. The base value is 100. Show your workings.
Food: weight 60%; price in base year €50; price in current year €55
Transport: weight 25%; price in base year €20; price in current year €24
Other Items: weight 15%; price in base year €75; price in current year €81
(12 marks)
model_answer:
Simple index = current price / base price x 100, then multiply by the weight.
Food: 55/50 x 100 = 110; 110 x 0.60 = 66.0
Transport: 24/20 x 100 = 120; 120 x 0.25 = 30.0
Other items: 81/75 x 100 = 108; 108 x 0.15 = 16.2
Composite index = 66.0 + 30.0 + 16.2 = 112.2
Prices rose by 12.2% on average.
marking_scheme: Part (a) total 32 marks; this part inferred at 12. Food: 55/50 x 100 = 110 x 60% = 66.0. Transport: 24/20 x 100 = 120 x 25% = 30.0. Other items: 81/75 x 100 = 108 x 15% = 16.2. Price index for the current year = 112.2.

prompt:
One role of the European Central Bank (ECB) is to formulate monetary policy for the Eurozone.
Explain the term monetary policy.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Monetary policy is the use of interest rates, the money supply and the availability of credit to achieve economic aims, mainly price stability. For the eurozone it is set by the ECB.
marking_scheme: Part (b) carries 22 marks; this part inferred at 6. Monetary policy refers to any action by the European Central Bank which influences interest rates, money supply and availability of credit for the Eurozone.

prompt:
The graph shows the Euro (€) to Pound Sterling (£) exchange rate: 01/09/2022: €1 = £0.90; 01/10/2022: €1 = £0.87; 01/11/2022: €1 = £0.86.
Does the prevailing trend on the graph indicate appreciation or depreciation of the Euro (€) to Pound Sterling (£)? Explain your answer.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Depreciation.
In September 2022, €1 bought £0.90. By November 2022, €1 bought only £0.86. Each euro now buys fewer pounds, so the euro has weakened (depreciated) against sterling.
marking_scheme: Part (b) carries 22 marks; this part inferred at 8. Answer: depreciation. Between 01/09/2022 and 01/11/2022 the rate falls from 0.90 to 0.86, so every euro is worth less, i.e. 86 pence instead of 90 pence.

prompt:
Should the Irish government be concerned if the Euro to Dollar exchange rate is appreciating? Yes or No. Justify your answer.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Yes.
A stronger euro makes Irish exports, such as Kerrygold butter or Aer Lingus flights, dearer for Americans. Demand for Irish exports and US tourism to Ireland may fall, hurting jobs in exporting firms. US imports become cheaper, so more money leaks out of the circular flow on imports. This can slow economic growth.
marking_scheme: Part (b) carries 22 marks; this part inferred at 8. Yes: price of imports decreases, so demand for imports may rise / greater leakages from the circular flow; price of exports increases, making Irish goods and services relatively dearer abroad and reducing demand for Irish exports. OR No: increased purchasing power / improved standard of living as people and businesses can better afford foreign goods/raw materials; reduced inflationary pressures.

prompt:
In budget 2023 the Irish government introduced a €600 electricity credit for all households.
Explain the main economic reason for the above government intervention.
(7 marks)
model_answer: To help households with the cost of living crisis. Electricity prices rose sharply, reducing real incomes. The credit protects living standards, especially for people on fixed incomes such as pensioners and social welfare recipients.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. Help citizens with the cost of living crisis / inflationary pressures; protect those on fixed incomes as they suffer most; prevent citizens' standard of living falling from the full increase in electricity prices; protect businesses facing rapid cost increases; market failure - supernormal profits from exploitation of consumers require redistribution.

prompt:
In budget 2023 the Irish government introduced a €600 electricity credit for all households.
Outline one possible economic disadvantage of this government intervention.
(7 marks)
model_answer: It is not means-tested. Every household gets €600, even wealthy ones that do not need help. This is not equitable, and the money has an opportunity cost: it could have been targeted at low-income households or spent on health or housing.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. Opportunity cost - funds could be used for another purpose; not means-tested - universal payments are not equitable as people who do not need support receive it; could lead to increased borrowing, affecting future generations; MNCs may distrust fiscal policy if they fear windfall taxes to fund it; electricity firms may continue earning large profits - better regulation could reduce prices instead.

prompt:
In budget 2023 the Irish government introduced a €600 electricity credit for all households.
In your opinion does the above government intervention encourage electricity users to reduce their use of electricity? Yes or No. Explain your answer.
(7 marks)
model_answer:
No.
Higher prices normally give consumers an incentive to use less. But the credit pays part of the bill, so households do not feel the full price rise. They can keep using the same amount of electricity without spending more, so there is little incentive to cut usage.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. Answer: No. As consumers can continue to purchase the same/similar amount of electricity without needing to increase their expenditure, they are likely to continue using the same amount. Regardless of price increases they feel protected by the government's electricity credit.

prompt:
Distinguish between the economic terms individual demand and market demand.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Individual demand: the quantity of a good or service that one consumer is willing and able to buy at different prices.
Market demand: the total quantity of a good or service that all consumers in the market are willing and able to buy at different prices. It is the sum of all individual demands.
marking_scheme: Part (a) carries 28 marks; this part inferred at 8 (2 @ 4). Individual demand refers to the quantity of a good or service an individual consumer is willing to purchase at various prices. Market demand refers to the quantity of a good or service all consumers in a market are willing to purchase at various prices.

prompt:
The Irish Government has provided free school transport for the 2022/2023 school year. Demonstrate, with the use of a fully labelled diagram the impact this new scheme will possibly have on the market equilibrium for petrol/diesel cars.
(15 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram: Price on the vertical axis, Quantity of petrol/diesel cars on the horizontal axis. An upward-sloping supply curve S. Demand curve D1 crosses S at E1 (P1, Q1). Demand shifts left to D2, crossing S at E2 (P2, Q2), with P2 below P1 and Q2 below Q1.
Explanation: free school buses are a substitute for driving children to school. When the price of a substitute falls (here to zero), demand for the good falls. Some households no longer need a second car, so demand for petrol/diesel cars falls at every price. The demand curve shifts left from D1 to D2. The equilibrium price falls from P1 to P2 and the equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.
marking_scheme: Part (a) carries 28 marks; this part inferred at 15 (diagram plus explanation, explanation points 8). Diagram: Price and Quantity axes, supply S, demand shifts left from D1 to D2, equilibrium E1 (P1, Q1) to E2 (P2, Q2). Explanation: the demand curve shifts left from D1 to D2; why - buses are substitutes for cars, so some households feel less need for a car and switch to free transport; equilibrium price falls from P1 to P2; equilibrium quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.

prompt:
The Irish Government has provided free school transport for the 2022/2023 school year. The rapid introduction of this scheme created an additional demand of 6,000 bus tickets in late September 2022 after schools had opened. Does this represent a government failure? Yes or No. Explain your answer.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Yes. The government intervened but did not plan for enough buses. Free tickets created excess demand, so 6,000 students could not get a place. This was an inefficient and unfair outcome caused by the intervention itself.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Yes: this government intervention created a more inequitable market for some consumers who were unable to access school transport due to government inefficiency.

prompt:
In 2006, multinational oil trading company Trafigura rejected an offer from a disposal company to deal with their toxic waste safely in The Netherlands for circa US$620,000. Instead they got a local company to dump it illegally in Cote d'Ivoire for just US$17,000 and in the process left more than 100,000 local people in need of medical assistance. (Adapted from amnesty.ie)
Does this represent a market failure? Yes or No. Justify your answer.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Yes. Market failure is inefficiency in the allocation of resources in a free market. Trafigura avoided the true cost of safe disposal. Instead, over 100,000 local people bore the cost through illness. This is a negative production externality the market did not price in.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Yes. Market failure occurs when the price mechanism in the free market leads to an inefficient / inequitable allocation of resources. The production has led to negative externalities for third parties - people not involved in production or consumption suffered pollution and ill health.

prompt:
The Circular Economy and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022 became law in Ireland in July 2022. The circular economy aims to transition away from the traditional 'take, make, waste' economy. (Adapted from gov.ie)
Outline two of the challenges the economy will face supporting the transition to the circular economy in Ireland.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
1. Consumer behaviour: many consumers are used to cheap, single-use products and may resist paying higher prices for sustainable alternatives.
2. Costs for business: firms must change production methods, packaging and product design to reduce waste. This raises costs in the short run and may discourage them.
marking_scheme: 8 marks: 2 @ 4. Consumer attitudes and behaviour - unaware of/unwilling to acknowledge their contribution to waste; consumers must be charged the full cost of products and may resist higher prices; government objectives - constant pursuit of growth may come at the expense of people and planet; business production methods - must change production, distribution and product life, which may increase costs; government needs to provide infrastructure, e.g. compost/recycling facilities.

prompt:
On average households in Ireland are responsible for 117 kg of food waste. The cost to households is between €400 and €1,000 per year. (Adapted from epa.ie)
Describe initiatives the Irish government could take to address the issue of food waste.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
1. Public awareness campaigns: advertising showing households how much money they waste, with tips on planning meals and storing food. This aims to change behaviour and meet the target of halving food waste by 2030.
2. A levy on bin waste: charging by weight gives households a price incentive to waste less and compost more. Local councils could also provide compost facilities.
marking_scheme: 10 marks: 1st @ 6, 2nd @ 4. Public awareness campaigns (national target of 50% reduction in food waste by 2030); increased funding for food waste charities, e.g. Food Cloud; National Food Waste Prevention Programme 2021-2027 (household, supply chain, hospitality); research (EPA research hub 'Facilitating a Green and Circular Economy'); a levy on bins to incentivise composting and less waste; local authority compost facilities.

prompt:
Deputy Barry Cowen described the argument that the agricultural industry 'must simply reduce the national herd (dairy and beef) to play its role as absurd'. (Adapted from gov.ie)
The argument for reducing the national herd (dairy and beef) is a controversial one. Outline one argument for and one argument against this proposal.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
For: agriculture produces about 32% of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly methane from livestock. Ireland must halve emissions by 2030. Missing EU targets means buying emission credits or paying fines, a cost to the taxpayer. A smaller herd is environmentally sustainable.
Against: it would hit the rural economy hardest. Farm incomes, jobs in processing and exports of beef and dairy would fall, reducing national income. New technology and farming methods should be tried first.
marking_scheme:
12 marks: 1st @ 7, 2nd @ 5.
For: beef industry in decline, dependent on subsidies, a large contributor to greenhouse gases; emission credit costs and EU financial penalties for missing targets; agricultural emissions are 32% of the national total; environmental sustainability - Climate Action Plan 2021 aims to halve emissions by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050 (agriculture target 22-30% cut by 2030).
Against: protection of the rural economy (urban vs rural bias); inequitable - agriculture is not the largest contributor (fossil fuels in homes and cars 38% in 2021); new mitigating technology should be trialled first; falling dairy prices already reduce farm incomes; fall in exports; employment effects.

prompt:
The Deposit Return Scheme is to be introduced in February 2024. Anyone who buys a drink will pay a small deposit for the plastic bottle or can container. Customers will get their money back when they return the container to a retailer or other collection point to be recycled. (Adapted from gov.ie)
Outline two likely effects the introduction of the Deposit Return Scheme will have on the Irish consumer.
(12 marks)
model_answer:
1. More recycling: the deposit gives consumers a money incentive to return bottles and cans instead of throwing them away. This works like the plastic bag levy, changing consumer behaviour and reducing waste and litter.
2. Higher upfront price: consumers pay more at the till. Some may buy fewer drinks in plastic bottles and cans, so demand for these products may fall.
marking_scheme: 12 marks: 1st @ 7, 2nd @ 5. Incentivises consumers to return containers / boosts recycling - old bottles and cans made into new ones, less waste; reduced use of scarce resources (plastic, aluminium, energy); reduced littering in public places - improved social infrastructure, less spending on cleaning; helps reach EU environmental targets; possible reduced demand as the price has increased, a disincentive for some consumers.

prompt:
The adapted infographic below displays data relating to Ireland's Balance of Payments on the Current Account for Q2 2023.
Goods: Exports €76bn, Imports €38bn
Services: Exports €91bn, Imports €83bn
(a) From the data above, calculate the balance of payments, current account balance. State whether it is a surplus or a deficit. Show all your workings.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
Total exports = goods €76bn + services €91bn = €167bn.
Total imports = goods €38bn + services €83bn = €121bn.
Current account balance = €167bn - €121bn = €46bn.
It is a surplus, because exports are greater than imports.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Workings: exports €76bn + €91bn = €167bn; imports €38bn + €83bn = €121bn; €167bn - €121bn = €46bn. Surplus.

prompt:
The adapted infographic below displays data relating to Ireland's Balance of Payments on the Current Account for Q2 2023.
Goods: Exports €76bn, Imports €38bn
Services: Exports €91bn, Imports €83bn
(b) Outline one advantage of having a surplus on the balance of payments.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Economic growth: a surplus means more money comes into Ireland from exports than leaves for imports. Exports are an injection into the circular flow of income. Through the multiplier, national income rises and the economy grows.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Possible advantages: increased economic growth (exports greater than imports, more goods and services produced, GNP per capita should rise); increased employment (more people needed to make exports, so jobs are created); taxation revenue (exports bring tax revenue to the Exchequer, and export workers pay direct tax); injection into the economy (exports are an injection into the circular flow of income, the multiplier increases and national income rises); attract FDI (MNCs may notice Ireland's success on foreign markets and locate here).

prompt:
According to Central Statistics Office (CSO) data, Ireland's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for October 2023 was 4.8%. This may be regarded as full employment.
(a) Explain what you understand by the term full employment.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Full employment is when everyone in the labour force who is willing and able to work can find a job at existing wage rates. Some people will always be between jobs, so in Ireland an unemployment rate of about 4% to 5% is seen as full employment.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Full employment is a situation when everyone in the labour force who is willing and able to work is employed at existing wage rates. In Ireland it usually occurs when the unemployment rate is between 4% and 5%.

prompt:
According to Central Statistics Office (CSO) data, Ireland's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for October 2023 was 4.8%. This may be regarded as full employment.
(b) Explain, giving two reasons, why full employment is an economic aim of the government.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
1. More tax revenue: people in work pay direct taxes such as PAYE and USC. They also spend more, so the government collects more VAT.
2. Less social welfare: fewer people need jobseeker's payments, so government current spending falls.
marking_scheme: 2 reasons @ 3 marks. Increased direct/indirect tax revenue (workers pay PAYE and USC; they have more disposable income to spend, which raises VAT); decreased social welfare payments (government current spending falls); boosts demand/economic growth (more disposable income to spend raises aggregate demand); reduction in poverty (earning an income raises the standard of living).

prompt:
According to Central Statistics Office (CSO) data, Ireland's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for October 2023 was 4.8%. This may be regarded as full employment.
(c) The achievement of full employment is an economic aim of the government. Explain how any other two current economic aims of the government may conflict with this aim.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
1. Price stability: with full employment, incomes and spending rise. Demand can grow faster than supply, causing demand-pull inflation.
2. Balance of payments: as Ireland is a small open economy, some of the extra income is spent on imports. This can reduce the surplus on the balance of payments.
marking_scheme: 2 aims @ 3 marks. Full employment vs price stability/control of inflation (more spending can cause demand-pull inflation); full employment vs balanced budget/control of state finances (more spending to keep full employment conflicts with balancing the budget); full employment vs balance of payments equilibrium (higher incomes in a small open economy mean more spending on imports, reducing the surplus); full employment vs housing for all (more demand for homes, but labour shortages, delays in supply and planning difficulties).

prompt:
During 2022, the equilibrium megawatt price per hour for electricity was €600. In an effort to combat the energy crisis, the European Commission considered a €200 per megawatt hour limit on the price of electricity.
[Diagram given: Price (MWh) on the vertical axis and Quantity of Electricity on the horizontal axis. Supply curve S and demand curve D cross at the equilibrium price of €600 and quantity Qe.]
(a) Illustrate, on the diagram below, how the European Commission's proposal above would alter the diagram.
(6 marks)
model_answer: Diagram in words: draw a horizontal line at €200 (P1), below the equilibrium price of €600. Where it meets the supply curve, mark the quantity supplied (Qs), which is less than Qe. Where it meets the demand curve, mark the quantity demanded (Qd), which is more than Qe. Label the gap between Qs and Qd 'excess demand' (a shortage).
marking_scheme: 6 marks for the diagram: a horizontal price line P1 at €200, below the equilibrium price Pe (€600). At €200 the quantity supplied is read off S (lower) and the quantity demanded is read off D (higher). The gap is labelled excess demand.

prompt:
During 2022, the equilibrium megawatt price per hour for electricity was €600. In an effort to combat the energy crisis, the European Commission considered a €200 per megawatt hour limit on the price of electricity.
(b) Explain your understanding of the economic term price ceiling.
(6 marks)
model_answer: A price ceiling is a maximum price set by law, usually by the government. It is set below the equilibrium price. Sellers cannot legally charge more than it. It protects consumers from very high prices, such as high energy bills.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. A price ceiling is a maximum price, usually set by a government, that can legally be charged for a good/service. It may be below the equilibrium price set by the market, but a firm cannot exceed it. It is put in place to prevent consumers being charged excessive prices.

prompt:
During 2022, the equilibrium megawatt price per hour for electricity was €600. In an effort to combat the energy crisis, the European Commission considered a €200 per megawatt hour limit on the price of electricity.
(c) In Budget 2024 the government announced energy credits of €450 for all households. Explain why you think the government introduced this credit.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
1. Cost of living: inflation and energy prices were very high. The credit cut every household's electricity bill, protecting living standards.
2. Fixed incomes: people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners and welfare recipients, lose the most purchasing power when prices rise. The credit helps protect them.
marking_scheme: 6 marks (scheme lists points marked 2 @ 3). Ease cost of living/improve standard of living (reduce electricity bills while inflation is high); protect fixed income holders (who suffered a big drop in living standards as energy costs soared); market failure (protect consumers from an unsatisfactory market price); war in Ukraine (part of a package of one-off measures to support households and businesses facing high energy prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine).

prompt:
(a) The table below shows a firm's capital to labour ratio for the previous two years.
2022: No. of machines 5, No. of workers 5, Ratio 1:1
2023: No. of machines 10, No. of workers 5, Ratio 2:1
From the information given above, tick one of the boxes below to indicate whether the firm has engaged in capital widening or capital deepening and explain your answer.
[Capital Widening] [Capital Deepening]
(6 marks)
model_answer:
Capital deepening.
In 2022 the firm had 1 machine per worker (5:5). In 2023 it has 2 machines per worker (10:5). The ratio of capital to labour has increased, so each worker has more capital to work with. This is capital deepening.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Capital deepening. In 2023 the firm employs 2 machines per worker compared with 1 machine per worker in 2022. Capital deepening occurs when an increase in the capital stock leads to more capital per worker.

prompt:
(b) Outline two factors which may affect an individual company's demand for labour.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
1. Demand for the firm's output: demand for labour is a derived demand. If more people want the firm's product, it needs more workers.

Upward sloping part:

prompt:
It has been estimated that in the Irish economy: MPT = 0.22, MPM = 0.30 and MPC = 0.6.
(b)(i) Based on the information stated above and using an appropriate formula, calculate the value of the multiplier in the Irish economy and explain the economic meaning of your answer. Show all your workings.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
Formula (open economy with a government sector): Multiplier = 1 / (MPS + MPM + MPT).
Step 1: MPS = 1 - MPC = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.
Step 2: MPS + MPM + MPT = 0.4 + 0.30 + 0.22 = 0.92.
Step 3: Multiplier = 1 / 0.92 = 1.087, about 1.08.
Meaning: every €1 injected into the circular flow of income, for example by government spending, increases national income by about €1.08. One person's spending becomes another person's income, so the final rise in national income is bigger than the first injection. The multiplier is small because a lot of extra income leaks out in taxes, imports and savings.
marking_scheme: 16 marks (scheme shows 12 for the calculation and 4 for the explanation; split inferred from the scheme layout). Method 1: MPS = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4; multiplier = 1 / (0.22 + 0.3 + 0.4) = 1 / 0.92; answer = 1.08. Method 2: 1 / (1 - (0.6 - 0.22 - 0.3)) = 1 / 0.92 = 1.08. Explanation: if there is an injection of €1 into the circular flow of income, national income will increase by 1.08 times; any initial injection of spending will cause a greater increase in the circular flow of income by 1.08 times.

prompt:
(b)(i) Explain, with the aid of a fully labelled diagram (including the axes), the long-run equilibrium of a firm operating in monopolistic competition.
(21 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram in words: Price/Cost on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal axis. Draw a downward-sloping AR (demand) curve and a steeper MR curve below it. Draw a U-shaped AC curve and a Nike-shaped MC curve that cuts AC at its lowest point. MC cuts MR from below at point E. Above E, at quantity Q, the AR curve just touches (is tangent to) the AC curve at price P, to the left of the lowest point of AC.
Explanation:
1. Equilibrium: the firm maximises profit where MC = MR and MC is rising (point E).
2. Output: it produces quantity Q.
3. Price: it charges price P, read off the AR curve.
4. Cost: cost per unit equals price at the tangency point, because AR = AC.
5. Profit: AR = AC, so the firm earns only normal profit. In the short run supernormal profits attracted new firms (no barriers to entry), which pushed each firm's demand curve down until only normal profit remained.
6. Efficiency: the firm does not produce at the lowest point of AC, so it is inefficient and wastes scarce resources.
marking_scheme: 21 marks: diagram plus explanation 12 x 1 (split for the diagram inferred). Diagram: P/C and quantity axes; downward-sloping AR and MR curves; U-shaped AC; MC; equilibrium E where MC = MR; AR tangent to AC at the price P to the left of the lowest point of AC. Explanation: 1. Equilibrium occurs at point E where MC = MR (and MC is rising faster). 2. Output: the firm produces Q. 3. Price: P. 4. Cost: shown at point C. 5. Profit: normal profit because AR = AC. 6. Scarce resources: the firm is wasting scarce resources / inefficient as it is not producing at the lowest point of AC.

prompt:
(b)(i) Explain the term income elasticity of demand.
(7 marks)
model_answer: Income elasticity of demand (YED) measures how responsive demand for a good is to a change in income. It is the percentage change in quantity demanded caused by a percentage change in consumers' income.
marking_scheme: Marks for this part not legible in the published scheme (inferred 7). Income elasticity of demand measures the percentage/proportionate change in the quantity demanded of a good caused by a percentage/proportionate change in consumers' income.

prompt:
(b)(ii) Using an appropriate formula and the figures in the table below, calculate the income elasticity of demand (YED) for this good. Explain the economic meaning of your answer. Show your workings.
2022: Average income €40,000, Quantity demanded 150 units
2023: Average income €50,000, Quantity demanded 180 units
(12 marks)
model_answer:
Formula: YED = (change in Q / change in Y) x (Y1 + Y2) / (Q1 + Q2).
Change in Q = 180 - 150 = +30. Change in Y = 50,000 - 40,000 = +10,000.
Y1 + Y2 = 40,000 + 50,000 = 90,000. Q1 + Q2 = 150 + 180 = 330.
YED = (30 / 10,000) x (90,000 / 330) = 0.003 x 272.7 = +0.82 (about +0.8).
Meaning: YED is positive, so this is a normal good - demand rose as income rose. YED is between 0 and 1, so the good is income inelastic: a 1% rise in income raises demand by only about 0.8%. The good is a necessity.
marking_scheme: Marks for this part not legible in the published scheme (inferred 12). Workings: +30 / +10,000 x (40,000 + 50,000 = 90,000) / (150 + 180 = 330) = +0.8. Explanation: the good is income inelastic - the percentage change in quantity demanded is less than the percentage change in income, so the good is a necessity (YED less than 1); it is a normal good - positive income effect, as income went up more was demanded.

prompt:
(b)(iii) Assume the income elasticity of demand (YED) for a PlayStation 5 is + 5.2 and total sales in 2023 were 10,000 units. Calculate the expected total sales for the year if consumers' incomes are expected to fall by 5% in 2024. Show your workings.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
% change in quantity demanded = % change in income x YED = -5% x 5.2 = -26%.
26% of 10,000 units = 2,600 units.
Expected sales in 2024 = 10,000 - 2,600 = 7,400 units.
marking_scheme: Marks for this part not legible in the published scheme (inferred 8). If income falls by 5%, sales are expected to fall by 5% x 5.2 = 26%. 26% of 10,000 units = 2,600 units. Expected sales = 10,000 - 2,600 = 7,400 units.

Discuss the economic advantages and disadvantages of increasing indirect taxation.
(12 marks)
model_answer:

Disadvantage: indirect taxes are regressive. They take no account of ability to pay, so people on low incomes pay a greater share of their income in tax. They also raise prices, which adds to inflation and may lead to wage demands.

Disadvantages: will increase inflation (and possibly wage demands); regressive/inequitable (lower income groups pay a greater proportion of income); revenue not as certain; burden of collection on retailers.

(6 marks)
model_answer: Cost benefit analysis means balancing up all the costs and all the benefits of a project (including external costs and benefits, now and in the future) before deciding whether to go ahead. Answer either (b) or (c)

prompt:
Answer either (b) or (c)
(c) Chocolate producers buy cocoa in advance of making products. In Q1, 2024, cocoa prices tripled. Manufacturers are expected to pass these higher costs on to shoppers and retailers in Q4, when most of the industry's sales are made around Halloween and Christmas. (Adapted from RTÉ News)
Do you regard the above situation to be an example of demand-pull inflation or cost-push inflation? Indicate your choice and justify your choice.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
Cost-push inflation.

Cost-push inflation happens when rising costs of production are passed on to consumers as higher prices. Here cocoa, a key raw material, tripled in price, so chocolate makers must pay more to make the same products and will pass this on to shoppers. It is not demand-pull inflation, because consumer demand has not risen faster than supply.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Answer: cost-push inflation. Justification: rising input costs (cocoa, a raw material); higher costs passed on to consumers as higher prices; not caused by a rise in consumer demand (demand-pull is 'too much money chasing too few goods'); a supply-side shock that reduces supply; time lag before prices rise is common with cost-push inflation.

prompt:
(a) Explain the difference between a positive economic statement and a normative economic statement.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
Positive economic statement: a precise, fact-based statement about how things are. It contains no opinion and can be tested or proved using data, e.g. 'The sugar tax has reduced demand for sugary drinks.'

Normative economic statement: a statement about how things should be. It is based on opinion and value judgements and cannot be proved with data. It often contains the word 'should', e.g. 'The government should raise the minimum wage.'
marking_scheme: 2 @ 3 marks. Positive: objective and fact-based; describes the world as it is or will be under certain conditions without value judgements; can be tested/verified using evidence/data. Normative: subjective, based on opinions/value judgements; expresses what 'should' happen rather than what is happening; cannot be tested/verified using evidence/data.
