Luxury: premium branded clothing. Justify: a non-essential product bought more as income rises; YED above 1 means income elastic demand - a % change in income causes a greater % change in demand in the same direction (YED +4.1: a 1% rise in income raises demand by 4.1%).

prompt:
(b) A study has shown that shoppers struggle to tell the difference between goods that have genuinely low impacts on the environment and those that are 'greenwashed'. (Adapted from the Irish Independent, May 2024)
(Greenwashing is a marketing measure / practice where some companies make false or exaggerated claims to appear more environmentally friendly than they actually are.)
Explain two ways in which greenwashing can lead to market failure.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
1. Asymmetric information: The company knows its product is not really eco-friendly, but the consumer does not. Because one side has more information, consumers cannot make informed choices, so the market fails to allocate resources efficiently.

2. Negative externalities: Greenwashed products may harm the environment more than buyers realise. This harm is not included in the price, so the products are over-consumed and society bears the external cost.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 3 marks. Information failure/asymmetric information (the firm knows the truth, consumers do not, so they cannot make informed choices); misallocation of resources (resources drawn away from genuinely green products; overinvestment in misleading products); reduced market efficiency (consumers pay premium prices that do not match true value; price signals disrupted); negative externalities/hidden demerit goods (harmful effects not shown in price, leading to overconsumption); erodes consumer trust/creates a 'missing market' (demand for genuine sustainable products falls).

prompt:
The diagram represents the long run equilibrium of a firm operating in an oligopoly market. [In the diagram, the curve labelled 2 is the average revenue (demand) curve, which has a kink at the current price P1.]
(b) With reference to the diagram, explain the shape of the curve labelled 2.
(6 marks)
model_answer:
Curve 2 is a kinked demand (AR) curve, because oligopoly firms are interdependent.

Above the kink (price above P1): if the firm raises its price, rivals do not follow. Customers switch to rivals, so quantity demanded falls a lot. This part is relatively elastic (flatter).

Below the kink (price below P1): if the firm cuts its price, rivals match the cut. The firm gains few extra sales, so this part is relatively inelastic (steeper). This explains price rigidity.
marking_scheme: 6 marks. Before the kink: if a firm raises its price, rivals will not follow; customers switch to competitors, so quantity demanded falls by a greater percentage than the price rise - this part of the demand curve is relatively price elastic. After the kink: if a firm cuts its price, rivals match the cut to avoid losing customers; the firm gains few new customers, so quantity demanded rises by a smaller percentage than the price fall - this part is relatively price inelastic.

prompt:
New health insurance provider, Level Health, to enter the Irish market this week. (Irish Independent, November 2024)
(a)(ii) With the entry of this new firm into the Irish health insurance market, outline two potential economic effects on the existing firms in the industry.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. Lower prices and lower profits: Level Health will try to win customers, so existing insurers such as VHI and Laya may have to cut their premiums to stay competitive. Lower prices mean lower profit margins, so they may need to cut costs and become more efficient. If Level Health undercuts them aggressively, a price war could cut profits across the industry.

2. Loss of market share and more non-price competition: Some customers will switch to the new firm, especially if it offers better deals to groups such as younger customers. To keep customers, existing firms may improve customer service, offer loyalty rewards or launch new products such as digital health services. This raises their costs but gives consumers more choice.
marking_scheme: 2 @ 7 marks. Possible effects: increased competition and lower prices (existing insurers lower premiums); improved services and innovation (better customer service, digital health services, personalised plans); market share redistribution (customers lost to Level Health, especially for firms with weak brand loyalty); pressure on profit margins (cut costs, streamline); regulatory and market responses (HIA monitoring; lobbying); potential mergers or exits of smaller insurers; increased consumer choice/market expansion; potential for a price war/short-term instability; impact on the labour market (job losses from cost cutting, or new jobs in marketing and customer service).

prompt:
(b)(i) A patent gives a pharmaceutical company the sole right to produce and sell a new drug. Explain, with the aid of a fully labelled diagram (including the axes), the long run equilibrium position of a pharmaceutical company operating in a monopoly market.
(21 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram (in words): Vertical axis 'Price/Costs (€)', horizontal axis 'Quantity'. Draw a downward-sloping AR (demand) curve. Draw a steeper MR curve below it, starting at the same point. Draw a U-shaped AC curve and a Nike-shaped MC curve that cuts AC at its lowest point. Mark E where MC cuts MR from below. Drop a line from E to the quantity axis: Q1. Go up from Q1 to the AR curve and across to the price axis: P1. Go up from Q1 to the AC curve (point Y) and across: C1. Shade the rectangle between P1 and C1 as supernormal profit.

Explanation:
- Output: the firm produces Q1, where MR = MC and MC is rising (profit-maximising).
- Price: it charges P1, read off the demand (AR) curve.
- Costs: average cost is C1. This is not the lowest point of the AC curve, so the firm is inefficient.
- Profit: AR is greater than AC, so the firm earns supernormal profits (area P1-C1-Y-X).
- Long run: the patent is a barrier to entry, so new firms cannot enter and the supernormal profits remain in the long run.
marking_scheme: 21 marks (diagram and explanation; the scheme shows 12 and 9). Diagram: axes Price (€)/Costs and Quantity; downward-sloping AR (= demand) curve; MR curve below AR; U-shaped AC curve; MC curve; equilibrium E where MC = MR; Q1; P1 read from the AR curve; C1 from the AC curve (point Y); minimum point of AC (W); supernormal profit area. Explanation: equilibrium is at E where MC = MR (and MC is rising); the company produces Q1; sells at P1; costs are C1 (point Y); it earns supernormal profits as AR is greater than AC; it is inefficient/wastes resources as costs are not at the minimum point of the AC curve (W).

Disadvantage: With no competition, the company can charge much higher prices for essential medicines and restrict output, so some patients may not be able to afford treatment.

More than three-quarters of the approximately 2,500 GP / doctor practices in Ireland have now closed their lists to new patients and over 700 GPs / doctors are due to retire in the next five years. (Adapted from RTÉ News)

prompt:
(c)(iii) The Irish healthcare system reflects Ireland's broader mixed economy. Explain what is meant by the term mixed economy and outline another example which shows that Ireland is a mixed economy.
(8 marks)
model_answer:
Mixed economy: an economy in between a command economy and a free enterprise economy. Goods and services are provided by both the state and private firms. Resources are allocated partly by the price mechanism and partly by government, through taxes, regulation, subsidies and public services.

Example: Transport. Irish Rail and Dublin Bus are state-owned, while private firms such as Go-Ahead Ireland also run bus routes.
marking_scheme: 8 marks. Mixed economy: an economic system that combines elements of central planning (government involvement) and private enterprise; resources are allocated by both market forces (supply and demand) and government intervention (regulation, public services, taxation, subsidies); most goods and services are produced privately but the government plays a significant role in essential sectors. Examples: education (public and private schools); transport (Dublin Bus state-owned, Go-Ahead Ireland private); energy (ESB/Electric Ireland competes with SSE Airtricity, Bord Gáis Energy, Energia); state regulation of private industries (regulators, ombudsmen).

prompt:

- The Irish government.

(7 marks)
model_answer: It will make the multiplier smaller (weaker). The multiplier works because one person's spending is another person's income. If workers put more of each extra euro into pensions, they spend less, so less income is passed on. In the formula Multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC), a lower MPC makes the denominator bigger and the multiplier smaller. E.g. MPC 0.8 gives 1/0.2 = 5, but MPC 0.75 gives 1/0.25 = 4. Any injection now raises national income by less in the short term.
marking_scheme: 7 marks. It will result in a weaker multiplier effect. Explanation: employees contribute to pensions so they have less disposable income to spend; the multiplier depends on spending (one person's spending is another person's income), so reduced spending means less job creation and slower growth; a lower MPC causes the denominator in the multiplier formula to increase, resulting in a smaller multiplier.

prompt:

Price €1.50: Quantity Demanded 40,000; Quantity Supplied 20,000
Price €2.00: Quantity Demanded 30,000; Quantity Supplied 30,000
Price €2.50: Quantity Demanded 20,000; Quantity Supplied 40,000
Price €3.00: Quantity Demanded 10,000; Quantity Supplied 50,000

(b)(ii) Using an appropriate formula, calculate the price elasticity of demand (PED) for Scentastic, when its price rises from €2.00 to €2.50 and quantity demanded decreases from 30,000 units to 20,000 units. Explain the economic meaning of your answer and show all your workings.
(14 marks)
model_answer:
Formula: PED = (change in Q / change in P) x (P1 + P2) / (Q1 + Q2)
Change in Q = 20,000 - 30,000 = -10,000
Change in P = €2.50 - €2.00 = €0.50
Step 1: -10,000 / 0.50 = -20,000
Step 2: (2.00 + 2.50) / (30,000 + 20,000) = 4.50 / 50,000 = 0.00009
Step 3: -20,000 x 0.00009 = -1.8
Answer: PED = -1.8

Economic meaning: The minus sign shows Scentastic obeys the Law of Demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls. The value 1.8 is greater than 1, so demand is relatively price elastic. A 1% rise in price causes a 1.8% fall in quantity demanded. The seller would raise revenue by cutting the price, not raising it.
marking_scheme: Allocation inferred as 14 marks (the published scheme does not show the full split). Workings: PED = (change in Q / change in P) x (P1 + P2)/(Q1 + Q2) = (-10,000 / 0.50) x (2.00 + 2.50)/(30,000 + 20,000). Answer: -1.8. Economic meaning: the sign is minus, so Scentastic obeys the Law of Demand (inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded); the absolute value is 1.8, which is greater than 1, so demand is price elastic - a percentage change in price causes a greater percentage change in quantity demanded.

(14 marks)
model_answer:
1. Increase market share: The owner may aim to sell as many smoothies as possible rather than maximise profit now. They could charge lower prices, run promotions, offer deals to local gyms and schools, or introduce new flavours. A larger customer base can bring economies of scale, lowering cost per unit in the long run, even though short-term profits are lower.

2. Satisfactory profit: The owner may be happy with a profit that gives a reasonable standard of living rather than the highest possible profit. For example, they might not open late every night, to keep a better work-life balance. Keeping prices fair also helps build a loyal customer base and avoids attracting new competitors.

prompt:
(b)(i) Retailers in the Irish fresh smoothie market can experience diseconomies of scale. Explain the term diseconomies of scale and outline one example which a retailer making fresh smoothies may experience.
(9 marks)
model_answer:
Diseconomies of scale are the cost disadvantages a firm faces when it grows too large: as output increases beyond a certain point, the average cost (cost per unit) rises.

Example: Communication and management problems. As a smoothie business opens more outlets and hires more staff, it becomes harder for the owner to communicate with everyone. It must pay extra supervisors and managers, which raises the cost of each smoothie.
marking_scheme: 9 marks. Diseconomies of scale: factors which lead to an increase in the average cost of production for a firm as that firm or its industry expands in size/as output increases. Examples: managerial diseconomies (communication problems, conflict, more supervisors); supply chain/storage problems (storing perishable fruit, waste); higher labour costs (supervision, training, lower motivation, staff turnover); increased rent/overheads; slower decision making; specialisation/division of labour leading to boredom and mistakes.

prompt:
(b)(ii) The partially completed diagram below shows how the costs for a smoothie bar change as it expands its operations over time. [In words: Costs on the vertical axis and Quantity on the horizontal axis, with two short run average cost curves, SRAC1 and SRAC2, already drawn.]

Explain the shape of the LRAC curve you have drawn: the downward sloping part of the LRAC curve and the upward sloping part of the LRAC curve.
(16 marks)
model_answer:
Diagram (in words): Keep SRAC1 and SRAC2. Draw SRAC3 to the right with its lowest point lower than SRAC2's (the lowest of all). Draw SRAC4 further right with a higher lowest point, and SRAC5 further right again, higher still. Each SRAC is a deep U. Draw the LRAC as a shallow U-shaped curve joining the lowest points of SRAC1 to SRAC5. Label the axes 'Average cost' and 'Output', each SRAC, and the LRAC. Mark Q3 below the lowest point of the LRAC.

Downward sloping part: Up to Q3, the LRAC falls because economies of scale are greater than diseconomies of scale. As the smoothie bar grows, it can buy fruit in bulk at a discount and use bigger, more specialised blenders, so cost per smoothie falls.

Upward sloping part: After Q3, the LRAC rises because diseconomies of scale outweigh economies of scale. For example, with many outlets, staff doing one repetitive task (only cutting fruit) become bored and less productive, and decisions slow down, so cost per smoothie rises.
marking_scheme: Allocation inferred as 16 marks. Diagram: axes Average cost and Output; SRAC1 to SRAC5, with their lowest points first falling and then rising; LRAC drawn as a shallow U joining/enveloping the SRAC curves; quantities Q1 to Q3 marked. Explanation: the downward sloping part of the LRAC (from Q1 to Q3) shows economies of scale are more dominant than diseconomies of scale (e.g. more specialised equipment reduces costs in the long run). The upward sloping part after Q3 shows diseconomies of scale are more dominant than economies of scale (a further example of a diseconomy, other than the one in (b)(i)).

prompt:
(c)(ii) In the short run a company may remain in business even if it is making a loss. Explain the meaning of this statement.
(5 marks)
model_answer: In the short run a firm must still pay its fixed costs, such as rent and insurance, even if it closes. If its revenue covers its variable costs (AR is at least AVC), it should keep trading. The extra revenue above variable costs helps pay some fixed costs, so its loss is smaller than if it shut down.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Even if making a loss, a firm should continue to operate in the short run if its total revenue (TR) exceeds its total variable costs (TVC)/if its average revenue (AR) is greater than its average variable costs (AVC). Any revenue above variable costs helps offset fixed costs, so the losses from continuing are less than the losses from shutting down.
